In this study, we identify all maximal curves with specific non-Hermitian characteristics that have multiple points with generalized Weierstrass semigroups of $\mathbf{3}\cdot 2^k + \mathbf{5}$, and compute the respective generalized Weierstrass semigroup at these points of interest.

Creating realistic singing voice recordings that sound natural is a complex task that deep learning models have successfully tackled in recent years. This research provides an in-depth analysis of the current deep learning-based methods for generating singing voices, covering various aspects such as data preparation, model designs, and performance metrics. We examine different model architectures, including attention mechanisms, generative adversarial networks, and their combinations, as well as the applications of deep learning models in singing voice synthesis. We also discuss the existing challenges and possible directions for future advancements in this field.

We introduce an expanded version of the NIPS4B dataset featuring 2000 audio recordings of 12 bird species, each labeled with 10-second labels for both song and non-song segments. This dataset has been split into two parts: one for training and testing purposes, and an additional dataset created for further data enhancement purposes. The latter includes an additional 5000 audio recordings, all of which were created using the same data collection and labeling method as the original dataset. These recordings can be accessed through an online platform, where users can also obtain real-time access to thousands of additional recordings, as well as a tool for automatically labeling their data, both of which are based on our open-source open-source code. The primary goal of this dataset is to serve as a resource for developing bird identification models, although it may also be applicable to other tasks.

Time-dependent event camera sensors record time stamps and data from
spatial locations upon each light detection, allowing for a diverse range of
applications. Although these cameras possess a high degree of flexibility in
addressing various tasks, their susceptibility to light leakage and
asynchronous readout mode generation can significantly hinder their
performance. Event camera sensors' inherent randomness in time and space
require the implementation of specialized methods to correct for light leakage
and timing inaccuracies. This work presents an innovative approach to
automatically correct event data, leveraging a unique combination of
geometric and probabilistic models. This method effectively addresses multiple
sources of inaccuracy, including spatial misalignment, light leakage, and
temporal discrepancies. We evaluate the approach on a diverse set of
datasets, encompassing driving, flying, and mechanical events, demonstrating
its ability to accurately estimate spatial and temporal inaccuracies and
produce high-quality, aligned event data, complete with associated timestamps.

Graphs have become a fundamental component in modern artificial intelligence systems, utilized in various applications such as social network analysis, computational biology, and recommendation systems. These applications rely on graph neural networks (GNNs) to extract meaningful information from graph structures. This survey provides an in-depth examination of graph neural networks, commencing with fundamental concepts and progressing to the latest developments in the field. We delve into the challenges inherent in graph representation learning, encompassing graph representation, structure, and dynamics. We offer a comprehensive overview of existing GNN methods and explore the underlying factors influencing their performance. Additionally, we discuss the evolution of GNNs and future directions for the field.

We provide a description of extraordinary collections within the moduli stack of degree two elliptic curves, specifically focusing on those over a field with characteristic zero.

At the end, an open question is raised regarding extraordinary collections for a general degree, assuming a certain conjecture holds.

Retinal surgery has become a viable treatment option for retinal diseases that traditional treatments cannot address. Although retinal surgery is complex and requires precise hand movements, current robotic systems lack the necessary 3D tracking capabilities. A novel approach is proposed to enable accurate tool direction tracking in retinal surgery by utilizing a beacon-based system. A miniature wireless tracker is integrated into the surgical tool to provide real-time 3D location data, which is then used to guide the surgeon's movements. An initial trial involving a simulated task demonstrated the effectiveness of this method, revealing a significant reduction in movement errors and improved tool precision.

The $F$-polynomial for a subgroup $H$ in a finite group $G$, denoted as $F_H(x)$, represents the count of $H$-conjugates of $x$. We establish two equations for $F_H(x)$ in relation to the $F_G(x)$ polynomials of $G$ and $H$. A previously discovered equation for $F_G^H(x)$ in relation to $F_H(x)$ and $F_G(x)$ applies to all finite simple groups $G$. Moreover, we demonstrate an equation for $F_G^H(x)$ and $F_H(x)$ applicable to simple unitary groups $G$, which generalizes a result by Ivanov and Kuribayashi.

The FIDO2 passportless authentication technology has garnered significant attention from multiple directions, but it remains unclear if the interest is justified - if so, or if it will eventually fade away; thus, this paper provides an objective standpoint on whether to adopt it widely or not.

The Weyl-Wigner formalism provides a comprehensive, operator-based description of discrete lattice systems, which can be applied to both bosonic and fermionic particles. This description is based on the momentum and space lattices, where the phase space is discretized into a grid of discrete momentum and space points. The Weyl-Wigner formalism offers several benefits, including a clear, operator-based representation, well-defined equations of motion, and a separation of dynamics between momentum and space. The formalism is particularly useful for maintaining unitarity and enforcing global quantum numbers, such as particle number conservation. The application of the Weyl-Wigner formalism to lattice systems is not limited to mean-field approximations; instead, it provides a general, analytical framework for solving lattice many-body problems. The formalism is also compatible with various approximations, including time-dependent Hartree-Fock theory and the time-dependent variational principle. The Weyl-Wigner formalism has been successfully applied to a range of systems, including Bose-Hubbard models, fermionic lattice gauge theories, and systems with spin-orbit coupling.

Current research on sense of agency (SoA) has mainly focused on specific stimuli, while this study explores how the platform's layout influences SoA in YouTube. A study was conducted with 120 participants, who watched 30 YouTube clips with varying layouts and then completed a SoA test. The results showed that SoA scores varied depending on whether videos were played on-youtube, space-youtube, or full-screen full-youtube and that these differences could be attributed to the user control and confidence associated with watching videos in distinct modes.

The pi-calculus, a well-established model for concurrent systems, is shown to be functionally complete in a strong sense. It can mimic the behavior of Turing machines through process communication, which involves renaming during synchronization. Building on this capability, we establish that the pi-calculus, when incorporating renaming within synchronization, can execute natural Turing machines with finite input and output outputs. Consequently, systems modeled with the pi-calculus, coupled with the integrated renaming operation, can perform an unlimited number of computations without getting stuck.

This paper presents a novel, explicit listing of code - a Gray code - covering all possible arrangements of n elements, represented by trees that have a fixed number of leaf nodes.  Notably, the list changes only minimally from one entry to the next, with the difference occurring in just one leaf position. Furthermore, the arrangement follows a clockwise rotation, a feature that has been explored previously in studies by de la Cruz, Enderton, and others, but the list has not been made publicly available.

The sPHENIX detector at RHIC utilizes a sophisticated magnetic solenoid to maintain precise particle tracking. During particle tracking, charged particles' paths are defined by the use of a helix model, where the starting point, velocity, and magnetic field are key variables. To enhance processing speed, sPHENEXP utilizes a high-performance GPU architecture. A new implementation of the ACTS library has been integrated into the sPHENEXP framework to enable efficient online tracking. This library was initially developed for LHCb and has undergone necessary modifications to accommodate the unique specifications of sPHENEXP. A comprehensive analysis of the library's performance on a single GPU has been conducted using simulated data, with an examination of factors such as accuracy, processing speed, and memory consumption. This analysis has demonstrated that the library's online tracking capabilities exceed in-operand requirements by a substantial margin, with an approximate 2-fold increase in speed.

This paper presents an enhanced computational method for evaluating the jump terms associated with the standard space-time finite element model, particularly in spatially constant diffusion coefficients. By leveraging the matrix-tree theorem, the resulting numerical inductance matrices possess a specific structure that facilitates efficient assembly in a block-diagonal format, enabling parallel computations. Furthermore, the method is adaptable to handle more complex cases where spatial coefficients vary smoothly and can be approximated through a spatial interpolation function.

This paper delves into circular current signatures in weighted, signed graph networks where edges have specific directions and labels, representing the overall flow pattern over a circular loop as a vector. We derive and prove the conditions under which circular current signatures either remain constant or can be made stable through minimal edge modifications. We also identify which edges are pivotal for maintaining circular current stability and demonstrate that any edge within a stable configuration can either remain unchanged or switch to the opposite direction. Additionally, we develop and provide specific algorithms for identifying and analyzing these key edges and derive conditions for determining when a particular edge will either sustain or flip its current signature when its direction is altered.

A specific type of distributed system is a modular subset total (MST) network, in which subsets of information exchanged between nodes are completely determined by the system's design. A deterministic version of this system, known as the modular deterministic subset total (MDST), has garnered significant attention. A key problem in this context involves calculating the minimum number of rounds required for all nodes in an MDST network to agree on a complete system, solution to which is of great practical importance. A prior solution to this problem was established in 2014 with a time complexity of 8 rounds, in the context of finite networks. This solution was built on the foundation of a broader algorithm developed for finite decision trees, in which a specific type of computation takes place. This study presents a new, finite MDST system solution that requires only 6 rounds, in addition to a new, broader algorithm for a specific type of computation that can be performed in 4 rounds. This new result is a direct extension of a computation model that was previously established in 2011. This new result is a direct extension of a computation model that was previously established in 2011.

Asteroseismic research into M-dwarf stars has been hindered by a lack of accessible data, but the 300 or more M-dwarf stars monitored by the ASAS-SN project offer a wealth of information, including photometric data that can be used to identify stellar bursts. By utilizing this data, researchers have identified 181 bursts in 141 M-dwarf stars and created a catalog of bursters. This catalog is a valuable resource for several reasons: it's the largest data set of stellar bursts to date, it includes the first information on 118 new bursters, and the bursts observed are some of the shortest ever recorded, lasting just a few minutes. This catalog's existence will aid in the identification of extragalactic bursters and inform future studies of stellar bursts.

During the early stages of an insect embryo's development, a specific type of blood cell called hemocytes migrate in a coordinated pattern during gastrulation, a crucial process that transforms the egg into a developing embryo. Recent studies have revealed that the movement of these hemocytes is influenced by a complex interplay of forces, including the structure of protein fibers called actin filaments, their rigidity, and the forces exerted by the embryo as it undergoes gastrulation. Using a combination of theoretical modeling and numerical simulations, researchers have developed a mathematical framework to describe the movement of these hemocytes in terms of the forces acting upon them, including the structural changes to their cell, the embryo's forces, and their interactions with the surrounding environment. By comparing the results of these simulations with actual observations of these cells in the developing embryo, researchers have confirmed the effectiveness of this new framework in predicting the complex behavior of these cells in the developing embryo.

In recent years, the field of speech-to-text conversion has made significant progress, primarily due to the effectiveness of sequence-to-sequence deep neural networks. However, the scarcity of labeled speech data in real-world applications continues to hinder the generalization of these models. This study explores the potential of using the Siamese network architecture in a semi-supervised learning context. By utilizing an auto-encoder-like setup, the Siamese network learns a shared latent space for both transcription and attendance tasks, facilitating cross-task knowledge transfer. Experimental results on the WSJ corpus demonstrate that our approach can produce comparable or even superior transcription results with minimal supervision, outperforming traditional unsupervised methods and achieving state-of-the-art performance under 10% labeled data conditions, while also achieving notable gains under 50% labeled data conditions.

We provide an update to our previous analysis, presenting new results for non-elastic lepton-nucleon scattering using a parametrization called SAID. This parametrization is based on the single-channel solution of meson-meson scattering and is combined with an elastic scattering model, allowing us to study different nucleon properties. We include recent data from MINERvA, E12-06-01, and SOLOLO, and use our model to calculate various scattering functions and distributions. We also explore alternative models, including the MAID framework, and our results are consistent with them.

This paper addresses the nearly certain stabilization issue for stochastic systems that switch between different regimes, where the regime is unknown and variable, and the objective is to adaptively manage adaptive control systems and estimate the system's parameters simultaneously. Specifically, it focuses on a specific type of stochastic systems, called regime-switching linear-quadratic systems, where the parameters can change over time, and it provides sufficient conditions for the nearly certain stabilization of these systems under adaptive management of both the controller and the parameter estimator. To achieve this goal, it introduces a specific Lyapunov function and applies it to both the continuous-time domain and the discrete-time domain, and it further generalizes the approach to the case of parameter-dependent matrices, where the parameters can change over time.

A comprehensive framework, active inference, offers a theoretical framework and computation mechanism for understanding and interacting with the environment through sensory data. While existing models have limitations in handling complex cases, this research develops novel computation algorithms that tackle these issues, including dealing with branching temporal lines, real-time interactions, and multiple sensory inputs. A key transformation technique enables these algorithms to be applied across various models in the branching tree structure, and their effectiveness is demonstrated through simulated scenarios.

We investigate how KdV solitons and perturbative perturbations evolve in a quenched, hadronic medium that interacts via gluons. The results show that KdV solitons maintain their energy and width throughout this process, while non-perturbative KdV solitons continue to spread, eventually equilating with the medium's thermal properties at a rate comparable to the energy release time of a single gluon plasma particle. Conversely, perturbative KdV perturbations propagate independently of the solitons' speed and cause the medium to gradually lose its non-equilibrium properties.

This research delves into the Eberlein-Grothendieck property in locally convex spaces, providing a comprehensive definition within the context of Banach spaces. We establish conditions under which a Banach space, or a locally convex space for that matter, satisfies this property, also offering insights into the underlying group structure. The study connects this concept to other established properties like property (a) and having a corner in the completion.

Our primary objective is to establish the conditions necessary for a planar system with one degree of freedom to be isochronic. Specifically, for a system with one degree of freedom, its planar Hamiltonian must be of the form $H(p,q) = \frac{1}{2}p^2 + V(q)$, with $V(q) = \frac{1}{2}v_1q^2 + \frac{1}{3}v_2q^3 + \frac{1}{4}v_3q^4$. Importantly, the coefficients $v_1, v_2,$ and $v_3$ are not subject to any constraints. Under these conditions, we find that if the system is isochronic, then the period of closed orbits is determined by the formula $T = \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{3}|v_2|}|E$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the constant $C$ in the estimate for the splitting of closed orbits is given by the formula $C = \frac{32|E|}{|v_2|}e^{-\delta}$, with $\delta$ being the smallest positive root of the equation $16|v_2\phi^3 + 4v_4\phi^4 + 2|v_5\phi^5 + 2|v_6\phi^6 = 2\pi$.

A novel approach, referred to as resemblance signature curves (RSC), is introduced to identify and distinguish unique patterns in continuous time series data, such as those found in the Lorenz system. Unlike conventional methods, the RSC method excels at identifying reduced-dimensional structures within data sets, even those consisting of high-dimensional data with noise, by relying on high-dimensional correlations rather than lower-dimensional representations. By quantifying the similarity between two patterns in a non-linear manner, the RSC method is capable of distinguishing distinct patterns in a step-by-step manner, allowing for the identification of specific patterns in a data set. Furthermore, the RSC method is capable of identifying and refining the parameters necessary to create desired patterns in the Lorenz system. By leveraging the RSC method, researchers can identify and analyze unique patterns in continuous time series data, even those with noise, by creating and refining the parameters necessary to create desired patterns in the Lorenz system.

The LAN property, typically associated with parametric statistical models, also applies to families of distributions of solutions obtained from Lévy driven SDE's, provided the underlying Lévy process exhibits finite activity.
We examine the possible outcomes of twisted Laplacians for forms, providing a simplified proof that their ranges are determined by a Teichmüller mapping as specified by Bell and Brumi\'er.

Fourier Neural Networks (FNNs), specifically FNet, are autoregressive neural networks that utilize Fourier Transforms (FTs) to eliminate tokens based on their complex frequency representations. Unlike traditional autoregressive transformer models, FNet leverages global information from the entire input sequence at once, thereby sidestepping sequential token processing. Consequently, FNet boasts a substantial speedup in training and inference, alongside preserved or enhanced accuracy. Nevertheless, FNet's reliance on FT introduces irregularities in the token elimination process, which hinders the model's capacity for global information utilization. To address this limitation, we introduce FNetAR, a novel autoregressive transformer model that integrates Fourier Transforms (FT) with global information from the input sequence. By incorporating FT within a transformer's recurrent architecture, FNetAR achieves a substantial speedup in training and inference, alongside improved accuracy. Moreover, the model's design allows for the incorporation of FT in a flexible manner, enabling the model to process tokens in a non-linear fashion. As a result, FNetAR exhibits enhanced capacity for global information utilization and outperforms FNet in a range of tasks, including language modeling and word prediction in the MMLM and CLM settings.

We examine the behavior of dark energy density in the universe within the framework of the GGPDE model in the context of the Saez-Ballester gravity theory. This theory is characterized by a scalar field, where the potential is governed by a function dependent on both time and a spatial parameter. We consider a spatial distribution of this parameter that reflects the spatial variation of dark energy density. We use the cosmological attractor method to find the cosmological attractor solution, where the spatial variation of dark energy density is represented by a function dependent on the scale factor. This solution leads to a cosmological model that can be described by a time-dependent potential. We then analyze the GGPDE model in this potential using the slow-roll conditions, where the spatial parameter is related to the spatial variation of dark energy density. We find that the GGPDE model exhibits a cosmological attractor solution that can be described by a time-dependent potential. This solution is consistent with the observed value of the dark energy density and the slow-roll conditions.

This paper proposes a two-stage approach to optimize mobile edge computing cloud service placement. First, a model is developed to determine the optimal number of edge nodes required to minimize energy consumption while meeting the recommended service density. This model is validated through experiments. Next, a training framework is designed to adjust the placement of virtual network functions on edge nodes to minimize energy consumption. To achieve this, a game-theoretic model is used to simulate the interaction between service providers and data centers. However, the model's non-cooperative nature leads to a challenge in finding a stable solution. To overcome this issue, a mean-field game model is used to simulate the interaction between service providers and data centers, and an algorithm is used to find a stable solution. This algorithm is then compared to other approaches in terms of convergence speed.

We investigate the characteristics of a Dirac fermion coupled to a stochastic $\mathbb{Z}_N$ symmetric mass using the renormalization group framework. The mass varies randomly between different values from the set $\{m_i\}$ as the energy scale changes, with each value chosen from the set with equal probability. Our findings indicate that the model exhibits a nontrivial fixed point in the large-$N$ limit for any number of $m_i$ values. Furthermore, we observe that the first-order transition changes to a second-order one when the number of $m_i$ values is greater than one.

The prevailing image of depression, based on medical studies and media portrayals, is that it brings only sadness and unhappiness. As a result, people living with the illness feel their experiences are not being accurately represented, leading to the assumption that depression is a condition without any positive aspects or benefits. This study aimed to challenge that perception by analyzing online posts from individuals struggling with depression who also shared moments of happiness. Through a detailed examination of their online content, the researchers identified patterns in the types of joyful events that people with depression often reported, and the factors that contribute to these positive events. The study also found that people with depression tend to focus on the emotional connections they have with others, rather than material or physical achievements. Ultimately, the research provides a more nuanced view of life with depression, highlighting the importance of relationships and the coexistence of difficult and joyful experiences.

We report findings from lattice simulations of a highly simplified Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) model, specifically the Sp(4) gauge theory with two distinct quark flavors, examining its behavior in both confining and deconfining phases using Monte Carlo simulations and calculating pion masses, decay constants, and low-energy constants. This research aims to validate a theoretical framework for QCD quark matter at finite temperature and density and assess its applicability in the context of the chiral limit, while also providing insight into the phase diagram of QCD. Our results confirm that the theory exhibits a pion mass that is directly proportional to the current quark mass, yielding a decay constant of approximately 5.5, similar to the value obtained in QCD. We also calculated the low-energy constant associated with pion-pion interactions and found it to be in line with expectations from chiral perturbation theory, suggesting that the theory's isospin symmetry is intact.

We investigated the magnetic properties of Na$_4$NiTeO$_6$ using magnetic susceptibility, electron spin resonance, and heat capacity measurements, and found it to be a unique compound with Ni$^{2+}$ ions exhibiting $S$ = 1 spin states. The material displays long-range magnetic ordering at 3.5 K, and exhibits distinct features in its ESR spectrum below the ordering temperature, indicating a type of magnetic arrangement. The material's heat capacity measurements also show a specific type of magnetic ordering, and the observed magnetization hysteresis indicates a first-order magnetic transition. Based on these results, we propose that Na$_4$NiTeO$_6$ has a zigzag arrangement of Ni ions, and the compound's unusual magnetic properties are likely due to the presence of a strong magnetic interaction between the Ni ions, as well as the influence of NiO$_6$ octahedra.

The concept of trust has been instrumental in shaping human behavior and decision-making processes, influencing whether we engage with others or provide assistance. Trust is a dynamic entity that evolves over time, influenced by various factors including reputation, social connections, and social standing. This research introduces a novel framework for building trust in intelligent transportation networks, which must navigate uncertain environments. Our proposed framework, grounded in Bayesian theory, assesses the credibility of other road users based on their actions and decision-making intentions. This framework not only considers the actions themselves but also the intentions behind them, allowing for a more nuanced understanding of trust. Through simulation results, our study demonstrates the practicality of this framework in evaluating trust in a scenario involving intelligent vehicles.

Cubic spline interpolation is a well-established technique for approximating functions that can effectively model piecewise-smooth curves with precise accuracy. However, when dealing with functions that present a sharp, high magnitude change in slope, the standard method tends to overestimate at regions of the steep gradient. This issue can be addressed by incorporating a monotonicity constraint, ensuring the approximated function maintains a consistent slope across the affected areas. Our research introduces a new algorithm, the monotonic cubic spline, specifically designed to tackle this problem by allowing the slope to increase or decrease, but not exceeding a predetermined threshold. This approach is capable of accurately modeling functions with multiple sharp changes and is computationally efficient, making it a viable option for various applications.

We explore a class of spacetimes within type IIA supergravity, comprising an $AdS_{4+1}$ bulk with a Taub-NUT internal sphere. The bulk spacetime features a time-like horizon, and we investigate the properties of scalar fields in its bulk. The scalar field's near-horizon behavior exhibits a unique feature: it reaches the top of the internal sphere at a finite distance from the horizon. Consequently, the field's behavior deviates from conventional behavior, where the field typically reaches a maximum at infinite distance from the horizon. The internal scalar field reaches its maximum at a finite radial distance, resulting in a distinctive feature near the horizon. This characteristic property enables the field to reach a maximum at a finite distance from the horizon, whereas conventional field profiles reach this maximum at infinite distance. The Taub-NUT internal geometry introduces a novel aspect: the scalar field reaches its maximum at a finite distance from the horizon. This distinctive feature can be attributed to the internal geometry rather than the bulk geometry. The field reaches a maximum at a finite distance from the top of the internal sphere, and this maximum is not solely determined by the bulk geometry. The internal geometry plays a crucial role in this process.

This paper presents initial findings from the Sound Categories Dataset project, aimed at developing sound classification systems. The project's long-term goal is to create a platform facilitating sound classification tasks such as annotation assistance, automatic processing, data enhancement, and classification training. A new dataset, the Sound Categorization Platform Dataset, has been developed by categorizing sounds into a hierarchical taxonomy and annotating them with the required attributes for classification training and superposition. The dataset is available for download on the project's GitHub page. This paper also discusses the project's short-term objectives, encompassing the development of tools for sound classification training and a web-based platform for crowd-sourced sound annotation.

A new model for studying complex ecological interactions, known as the dynamic mean-field theory (DMFT), offers an efficient and accurate approach. This model involves transforming interconnected systems into simpler, non-local frameworks, preserving their key characteristics. By focusing on the dynamics of population growth, the DMFT equations can be easily derived and solved to analyze the systems' behavior. This model can be applied to both individual species and groups of species interacting with each other through predation, competition, or other mechanisms. As it relies on the average population sizes, the DMFT equations can be simplified and solved analytically in certain cases, such as mean-field theories. In contrast to other approaches, the DMFT allows for a more accurate representation of abrupt transitions in population growth, as it incorporates the effects of non-linear interactions. By using the DMFT framework, researchers can investigate the behavior of complex ecological systems, including the impact of multiple interacting factors, as well as the emergence of new, stable states.

The concept of a Cayley tree system, composed of a central node connected to a finite number of subnodes, has been applied in various contexts, including information theory, social network analysis, and random matrix research. In this study, we examine the properties of a Cayley tree system with independent, identically distributed edge weights, where the distribution of the central node's weight influences the system's behavior. In the subcritical regime, where the central node's weight exceeds a certain threshold, we demonstrate that the system's edge weights follow a stable distribution with a characteristic index between 1 and 2, depending on the central node's weight. Our findings have implications for the system's avalanche statistics, including the size distribution of avalanches and the relationship between avalanche size and central node weight. Notably, in the subcritical regime, we observe a power-law tail in the avalanche size distribution with an index less than 2, a phenomenon not previously documented in the literature.

The task of dialogue understanding involves generating responses to given sentence pairs, which are considered as dialogue contexts. To achieve this, we've developed a query response framework that leverages pre-trained language models to represent these sentence links. Our framework consists of a sentence embedding component that generates vector representations for both input and dialogue contexts, and a response generation component that produces output based on these embeddings. To further enhance our framework, we've integrated a dependency parsing layer, which utilizes dependency relationships between dialogue context sentences to refine our sentence embeddings. Our model's effectiveness is demonstrated through its evaluation on the publicly available CoQA dataset, which showcases its ability to excel in both open-ended and multiple-choice question answering tasks.

This review focuses on the mathematical properties and numerical approximation of the flawlessly aligned (FAM) layer, specifically in the context of transmission problems involving hyperbolic partial differential equations. FAM is distinct from the previously established flawlessly aligned (FLA) layer with a complex value at the boundary that enables smooth hyperbolic wave transmission. Unlike FLA, the FAM layer consists of a real-valued function that achieves the same objective, often arising from specific generalizations of the perfect matched layer (PML) with a complex coefficient. We examine the properties of this FAM layer in various numerical methods for solving time-domain hyperbolic wave equations.

Researchers have been studying how a jet of gas ejected from a droplet array responds to interacting with a laser pulse jet. This involves modifying a droplet's surface with a CO$_2$ laser pulse, causing it to deform and break apart into smaller droplets that merge with adjacent droplets in the array, resulting in the formation of new smaller droplets. This process continues until the droplets deform and break apart due to the gas jet's force, leading to the formation of even smaller droplets that merge and deform the array. This process can be repeated, allowing for the deformation and fragmentation of the array, and ultimately enabling the creation of very small droplets. This phenomenon has potential applications in the precise control of fuel droplets in engines, as well as in inkjet printers using water-based inks.

The rapidly expanding Internet of Things (IoT) network generates immense amounts of data from a multitude of devices, necessitating the development of sophisticated traffic management techniques to ensure efficient and reliable data transmission. This research introduces an innovative approach utilizing Software-Defined Networking (SDN) to manage IoT data traffic, dividing the network into distinct sub-networks for IoT devices and a central network handling control and management functions. This architecture exploits the benefits of pub/sub architectures, enabling SDN controllers to efficiently direct IoT devices to appropriate sub-networks for optimal data transmission. Our proposed framework has been validated through simulations, yielding significant reductions in packet loss, delay, and network congestion, demonstrating its superior performance compared to conventional techniques like WLEAD and weighted round-robin strategies.

LkH$\alpha\,330$ is a T Tauri star surrounded by a substantial amount of gas and dust surrounding its protoplanetary disk. Recent observations of this star and surrounding environment have revealed distinct variations in dust and gas density, which are thought to indicate the presence of a planetary system. The analysis of dust and gas distributions in the system suggests that the dust is primarily composed of particles with a maximum size of approximately 1 micron. The presence of these particles, along with gas, is believed to result from the formation of planets in the star system. The observed dust size distribution in the system is consistent with theoretical models of protoplanetary disk evolution, particularly in the spirit of the core accretion scenario. The dust in the system is primarily composed of silicates, a finding that is consistent with expectations. The presence of dust in the star's disk is thought to be the result of a combination of factors, including the fragmentation of large dust particles and the presence of dust generated by the erosion of dust grains in the system.

This paper introduces a metric that associates with a vector space of positive definite matrices. The main objective is to develop a metric that facilitates the computation of geodesics in a manifold embedded within an expanded domain of positive definite matrices. To achieve this, we define a vector-valued function operating on the Lie group of invertible matrices, enabling the derivation of a differential operator necessary for defining a metric. Subsequently, we define a vector-valued metric and show that its associated geodesic is a matrix exponential. Finally, we establish that the geodesic satisfies the properties of a gyrogeometric curve.

The European Union's aspiration for a carbon-neutral energy system, as stated in the European Green Deal, can be achieved by 2050. Accomplishing this target requires significant efforts to transform the energy sector, replacing fossil fuels with renewable sources and hydrogen, which can serve as a versatile energy carrier in this process. As a result, hydrogen production is expected to increase in the future. This paper outlines the benefits of establishing a hydrogen network in Europe. Initially, the initial costs associated with hydrogen production and storage will be high, but they will decrease over time. The study utilized the $NEMO$ model to examine the optimal hydrogen network in Europe, taking into account various scenarios. The findings indicate that the hydrogen grid is a viable option for a carbon-neutral energy system, as demonstrated by the optimal European hydrogen network design. The initial investment required for the hydrogen network is approximately 0.5 billion euros, but this initial cost can be recouped through the sale of 1 TWh of hydrogen within 20 years. The initial investment required for the hydrogen network is approximately 0.5 billion euros, but this initial investment can be recouped through the sale of 1 TWh of hydrogen within 20 years.

The origin of subsurface horizontal magnetic fields (HMFs) is a long-standing mystery in our understanding of the solar atmosphere. These fields are a key component in models of solar dynamos, but their exact source remains unknown. We propose that subsurface HMFs contribute to the anisotropy observed in the travel time of solar waves, offering a potential method for uncovering the underlying cause. We simulate the effect of HMFs on solar wave travel time using a 3D solar dynamo model and find that it closely matches the actual travel time data. We also discover that the anisotropy in wave speed can be used to infer the strength of subsurface HMFs, potentially allowing for direct observation of these fields through seismological measurements.

We propose a novel approach to protecting entangled photons transmitted through a photonic chip by leveraging topological encoding. An innovative design combines two techniques - squeezing and topological protection - to maintain robust entanglement despite noise within the chip. Our method is based on the Kitaev's toric code model, in which each qubit is represented by two photons, resulting in a robust entanglement even against phase-flip errors. This scheme offers the potential for expansion, incorporating multiple encodings and enhanced security through quantum error correction, thereby mitigating the effects of environmental noise.

Time-critical applications, such as emergency response and drone swarms, demand quick execution of complex tasks. Although motion planning techniques can generate efficient paths, they often result in numerous possible trajectories. Selecting the optimal path is a computationally demanding process, particularly when numerous alternative routes are available. This paper introduces a novel approach, called Fluid Time Efficient (FTE), which generates smooth, continuous paths in a given time frame. Unlike conventional methods, FTE is computationally efficient and can produce a single, optimal trajectory within a short time frame, thereby addressing the complexity of time-critical applications.

This study proposes a novel class of codes known as q^2-linear conjugacylic codes, which operate within the finite field F(q^2). This type of code is generated through two distinct linear codes, and the proposed algebraic structure is utilized to establish a specific decomposition of the group Z_4. Furthermore, an equation is developed to calculate the minimum distance of these codes, and it is demonstrated that this minimum distance is at a minimum of 6. Additionally, an investigation into the duals of these codes reveals that they are isomorphic to various subsets of the toric codes, and an explicit formula is provided for the duals of these codes. Ultimately, it is shown that the dimension and number of codewords within a q^2-linear conjugacylic code are dependent on the parameters of the two generating linear codes, and an example is provided to illustrate this principle.

This report outlines the findings of the Snowmass 2021 thematic group on career pipeline and career advancement, focusing on career paths in physics. Key discoveries and future research objectives are presented.

This study examines the polarization of W bosons in tbar-t events generated from 8 TeV proton-proton collisions at the ATLAS detector at the LHC using a 20.2 fb-1 dataset. The research utilizes the lepton-plus-jets channel with tbar-t pairs reconstructed from either electrons or muons, and subjects the data to various requirements including at least one isolated, high-transverse-momentum lepton and two or three jets. The study employs a multivariate technique to distinguish W boson polarization and measures polarization components, including sigma_p_T / sigma + sigma_z / sigma, for both electrons and muons, as well as the overall polarization ratio f_3 / f_1 + f_3 / f_2. The results are compared to Standard Model predictions, and within the experimental and theoretical uncertainties, show compatibility.

The heavy flavor production process in hadron collisions is an effective means of studying charm and beauty quark dynamics. The $D$-meson's parton distribution functions, specifically its longitudinal and transverse components, are crucial in understanding this process. By examining the $D$-meson's rest frame and longitudinal motion, researchers have reevaluated its twist-2 and twist-3 distribution amplitudes, as well as the $g_{4}(u)$ parameter, through the application of QCD light-cone sum rules. The results of this analysis have been compared to previous studies, revealing new insights into the $D$-meson's geometric structure.

This paper demonstrates that the power graph's spectrum, determined by its adjacency matrix raised to any positive power, encompasses the spectrum of both the power hypergraph and its corresponding signed graph. This connection allows us to find the spectrum of the power hypergraph based on the spectrum of the power graph. We further utilize the power graph's spectrum to devise an eigenvalue localization theorem for the power hypergraph, along with providing examples to illustrate this concept.

The impact of various sources of interference on the Global Navigation Satellite Consortium is examined, considering factors like increased satellite numbers, rising traffic volumes, and rising power levels from external sources.  An analysis of the trade-offs between the network's ability to provide accurate positioning data, to maintain its minimum coverage threshold, and to keep signal power within acceptable levels is presented.  An assessment of the interference generated by the planned Starlink constellation on the QPSK signals from the European Geostationary Navigation Alliance satellite is conducted.  Findings show that the Starlink network's technology can meet current navigation requirements, but only by significantly boosting onboard receiver sensitivity, achieving a 50-decibel gain over the European Geostationary Navigation Alliance receiver.  An assessment of the Starlink network's ability to provide positioning data with desired levels of accuracy is conducted, revealing that the minimum power threshold can be met using a receiver sensitivity level that is 32 dB below the European Geostationary Navigation Alliance receiver.

The variation in transit timing is a valuable tool for analyzing the internal structure and orbit of exoplanets. By analyzing 27 transit events of the hot Jupiter planet XO-3b, we discovered that the variation in transit timing is directly proportional to the planet's semi-amplitude of the orbit. This suggests that the gravitational interaction between the planet and its host star can be accurately described by a quadrupole term, indicating a high level of tidal development. Additionally, our study found that the transit timing variation matches a theoretical model of an eccentric orbit, further supporting the theory that the planet formed in a highly eccentric state and developed into its current state due to tidal interactions with its host star.

The 21-cm global 21-cm emission is a valuable tool for understanding the large-scale cosmic evolution, and it is particularly useful for studying the effects of the Milgrom acceleration on the cosmic evolution. However, this signal is easily disrupted by various astrophysical effects, such as the formation of stars and the conversion of gas into stars. These disruptions significantly impact our understanding of the cosmic evolution. In this study, we present a new method for accurately measuring the amplitude of the 21-cm global signal at any given time. Our method is based on a Bayesian calibration technique and takes into account the effects of these disruptions. Our results show that the new method is more effective than traditional methods in accurately measuring the amplitude of the 21-cm global signal. As a result, this new method will significantly improve our understanding of the cosmic evolution.

This research examines relative Gromov-Witten invariants of geometric bundles and their symplectic transformations, providing a general framework that covers various bundles with specific characteristics. The approach involves adapting Ruan's open-closed approach to study relative Gromov-Witten theory in bundle coordinates. The resulting proof is structured around three key components: establishing the K\"ahler-Riemann-Hilbert problem, verifying the potentiality of the constructed generating function, and proving its convergence. Additionally, the paper investigates the limiting behavior of the Gromov-Witten invariants as the bundle's rank approaches infinity.

We derive major breakthroughs on the distribution of various arithmetic functions within short intervals. Notably, we establish simultaneous prime number theorems for a wide range of functions while maintaining an exceptionally uniform distribution. Leveraging our novel approach to averaging, we obtain the first results that closely mirror the weak form of the Lindelof hypothesis.

In clinical trials for Alzheimer's disease, researchers often rely on cognitive function tests to gauge improvement.  Traditional methods of analyzing these trials compare change in cognitive function between treatment groups, but this approach can be misleading due to uneven distribution of missing data between groups.  A more effective method is to estimate individual subjects' data, but this approach can be time-consuming and resource-intensive.  A new approach, using a mathematical model known as a natural cubic spline, may offer a practical and efficient solution by pinpointing specific cognitive functions that show the most noticeable improvements.  This method has been successfully applied in a study analyzing data from a clinical trial, and the results indicate that it may provide more accurate information than previous methods.

This paper outlines an innovative approach to gathering data for parking system development, known as CRAWLING. By leveraging the potential of crowdsourcing, CRAWLING allows users to contribute real-time parking information while receiving rewards, making it a valuable resource for users and beneficial for parking service providers. Our proposed prototype, CRAWLING, consists of three primary components: mobile apps, parking lot servers, and a data analysis platform. These elements work in tandem to ensure the accuracy of user-submitted information, provide incentives, and streamline parking assignments. Our early-stage pilot test yielded promising results, demonstrating the feasibility and effectiveness of CRAWLING.

Level Minima Optimization, a type of gradient-based optimization technique, has been found to offer a stable and efficient approach. However, previous research suggested that Level Minima Optimization may not always perform optimally, even when utilized with the Stochastic Gradient Descent algorithm. To address this issue, we have developed a new theoretical framework that identifies specific conditions under which Level Minima Optimization successfully converges when applied to a common class of machine learning models. Furthermore, our study reveals that Level Minima Optimization can achieve convergence in more complex cases if certain conditions related to the data, the neural network architecture, and the learning rate used are satisfied. To verify the practical value of our findings, we have conducted extensive experiments that validate the effectiveness of Level Minima Optimization across various machine learning tasks.

A cutting-edge approach to parametric amplifiers involves reflective designs that offer improved frequency selectivity and increased gain. However, past implementations of these designs have been limited by the lack of available power for the nonlinear element, thereby restricting the frequency selectivity. This paper presents a novel design for a parametric frequency selective attenuator that leverages reflective architecture to achieve a high dynamic range while minimizing loss to near zero using only milliwatt levels of input power.

The SEIRS compartmental epidemiological model is used to analyze the COVID-19 outbreak, assuming no pre-existing immunity. This model is characterized by five interconnected components: susceptible, exposed, infectious, recovered, and deceased populations. A key aspect of this framework is its ability to capture the inherent delay in the recovery process, which leads to a distinct time-scale disparity between the onset of infection and the return to normalcy. This framework is applied to the Cantor set, using self-similar model equations, to simulate the COVID-19 outbreak in regions with high levels of transmission. This approach allows for the identification of the Cantor set's critical dimensions, which correspond to the transition periods from a growing epidemic to a stable, sustained outbreak. An alternative method, based on the use of the inverse of the next-generation matrix, is employed to derive a system of ordinary differential equations modeling the COVID-19 outbreak. This system is used to calculate the basic reproduction number and to simulate the impact of different intervention strategies on the pandemic's trajectory.

We suggest a method for selecting the most suitable word context embedding among multiple options, based on the specific requirements of the input task. The proposed system combines concepts from active learning and attribute-based decision-making, presenting a selector that determines an optimal word context from a pre-constructed set of word embeddings, choosing either improved, good, or the best possible option. The system is particularly effective when data is scarce and can be applied to various natural language processing tasks such as text classification, without needing to train a model. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by achieving high accuracy rates in multiple binary text classification tasks, outperforming existing methods.

We examine the $k$-group distribution for a high-density non-regular random geometric graph, and we find that it converges to a Poisson distribution as the density of the graph increases indefinitely.

The Lagrangian method is a powerful tool for modeling the evolution of isolated stars that have undergone core collapse, primarily because it can directly simulate the behavior of the star's fundamental components. Although the method's effectiveness in describing non-rotating stars is well-established, its application to rotating stars is relatively unexplored. To address this gap, we have developed a Lagrangian model that can incorporate the effects of rotation, thereby enabling the analysis of a wider range of astrophysical phenomena related to rotating stars. To validate our approach, we have applied our model to a specific scenario involving the collapse of a rotating protostar. Our results indicate that the model can successfully replicate the protostar's collapse into a black hole, and we have observed the emergence of a complex, spiral-shaped shockwave during the process, which is in agreement with predictions made by other Eulerian models. Furthermore, we have found that the protostar's angular momentum is transferred to the surrounding matter through the formation of helical structures during the shockwave's propagation.

A spacetime model known as the generalized Lema\^{\i}tre-Tolman-Bondi (gLTB) spacetime is studied under the Palatini $f(R)$ gravity, where $f(R)$ is a smooth function of the Ricci scalar $R$. The spacetime is characterized by three key parameters: the radial coordinate $	ilde{r}$, the metric potential $m(	ilde{r})$, and the scale factor $v(r)$. This analysis reveals that the spacetime is singular at the origin $	ilde{r}=0$ for non-flat three-geometries and at the origin $	ilde{r}=0$ and $	ilde{r}=r_H$ for flat three-geometries. The spacetime model is also singular at the curvature radius $r=r_H$ for non-empty models, and this singularity is of type C in all cases. The matter-energy conditions are examined, and it is found that the strong energy condition holds for the matter field in the spacetime model. The Ricci scalar $R$ and Ricci tensor $R_{\mu
u}$ are studied in detail, and their properties are analyzed. The analysis also includes the study of the energy-momentum tensor $T_{\mu

u}$, and the Ricci tensor $R_{\mu
u}$, as well

Quantum nonlocality holds a pivotal position in the development of quantum information theory. In this research, we investigate the quantum nonlocality of systems comprising N parties and N-2 measurement settings. We demonstrate that any N-partite state, regardless of complexity, will exhibit robust quantum nonlocality when the number of measurement settings exceeds N-2. Conversely, simple product states always pass this test. Robust quantum nonlocality cannot be achieved with less than N-2 settings. We further establish that certain N-partite states exhibit robust quantum nonlocality across all N, whereas other states may not.

To enhance our understanding of how people interact with digital content, researchers have developed a method to continuously analyze where users focus their attention while browsing the web. This method utilizes existing eye-tracking data to identify the users' primary areas of focus and updates this information in real-time, taking into account where the user last focused their attention. The eye-tracking data is stored in a time-series format within a database, and our method applies a Gaussian Mixture model to identify distinct user behavior patterns. These patterns are then used to identify specific user subgroups, and our approach continuously updates these subgroups based on new data. This method has been implemented using data from the "WebEye" eye-tracking database, and our findings demonstrate that it accurately identifies users' primary areas of focus.

Recent breakthroughs in millimeter-wave (mmWave) communication technology have
led to the exploration of new communication systems operating in even higher
frequency bands. Terahertz communication, which involves frequencies above 100
GHz, is a promising area of research with tremendous potential for future
wireless networks. In this research, we explore the concept and application of
terahertz communication in the 0.3-10 THz range, with a focus on the development
of a novel terahertz reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) that utilizes
polymeric electro-optical crystals. The RIS's ability to dynamically adjust its
transmission parameters through external electrical signals and optical exposure
makes it an attractive solution for terahertz communication systems. We have also
developed a prototype of the RIS using commercially available components.

Offline reinforcement learning focuses on solving complex decision-making problems using past experiences, which can now be leveraged even after the event has concluded. Building upon previous research, state-of-the-art methods for offline RL have utilized the linear programming structure in conjunction with Bellman optimality conditions to develop efficient solutions. However, this approach is limited to scenarios where the state and action spaces are finite and where the state and action dimensions remain low. In contrast, this study proposes a new method that lifts these constraints by incorporating general function approximation methods, specifically random feature maps, to tackle offline RL problems. Our method relies on the Q distribution property, a novel condition that generalizes the Bellman optimality condition to accommodate non-uniform probability distributions. By framing the problem as a linear optimization task and utilizing Q distribution-based constraints, our method offers a more comprehensive approach to offline RL. In our experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this novel formulation across various offline RL problem settings.

We demonstrate that the homotopy category of a given infinity category is
determined by its path categories. Furthermore, we show that the path categories of an
upper Haskoif category X, specifically those that support weak path compositions, 
are in one-to-one correspondence with its possible quasi-functorial weak factorization
systems.

A long-standing mystery has surrounded supermassive black holes, whose masses have been steadily increasing over time. Despite numerous attempts, researchers have struggled to identify the process that fuels this growth. However, recent observations of distant galaxies have revealed that there is no significant evidence supporting the theory that supermassive black holes feed on intergalactic material. Instead, it is possible that supermassive black holes are actively consuming material from their own stars. In this context, we conducted a theoretical study to examine the dynamics of a supermassive black hole consuming its own star material. Our findings suggest that this process causes a significant increase in turbulence within the galaxy, which can slow down the rate at which the black hole consumes material. In some cases, this turbulence can be so intense that it can actually stop the growth of the black hole. Our research has also shown that galaxies that contain a supermassive black hole will display a range of distinct features, including a lack of star formation, an unusual rotation pattern, and a significant increase in the speed at which stars orbit around the black hole's event horizon.

This study delves into specific line-based configurations that arise in the context of the planar three-body problem. In this scenario, we define a set of mutually gravitational attractive forces acting between three objects in a two-dimensional space. We examine two distinct arrangements, which we term "chain" and "Y", and investigate their occurrence patterns as the problem evolves over time. Our goal is to identify the conditions under which these configurations occur and assess their prevalence in the system's behavior.

Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) is a cutting-edge technique used to generate three-dimensional, fluorophore density maps based on their decay times. This approach relies on time-tagged charge-coupled device (TTCC) cameras, which record the arrival times of photons with high precision. As a result, FLIM data are represented as sparse matrices of time-tagged values, in contrast to traditional fluorescence imaging, which employs intensity data. This unique format enables the application of sophisticated deconvolution algorithms to improve FLIM's resolution. This article provides an in-depth review of FLIM, its data representation, and the implementation of deconvolution methods to enhance FLIM's capabilities for imaging small specimens.

Product search systems are essential for e-commerce websites, offering users an efficient way to locate products matching their interests. To provide users with a personalized search experience, an e-commerce company analyzes its customers' behavior patterns, including past searches and browsing history. To achieve this goal, our research presents a novel approach that predicts a user's current actions based on their historical interactions with the website. By utilizing a graph neural network to model a user's activity, our method can generate a search query or action prediction. To optimize our model, we created a training technique that adjusts the edges between activities in a user's graph, allowing for a more accurate prediction of their actions. Our method's effectiveness was demonstrated through its application in a personalized search system for an e-commerce company, resulting in a significant 7.3% boost in search results relevance. Our research was the first to apply a graph neural network to a large-scale e-commerce company's user data, offering insights into the potential applications of this technology.

Graphs containing numerical data are frequently represented in a condensed format using graph embeddings, which can then be processed by text-based models. However, existing graph embedding techniques often rely on labeled data, which can be scarce in real-world applications. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel unsupervised deep learning approach called Unsupervised Manifold Characterized Graph Embedding (UMCE), capable of generating node embeddings without labeled data. UMCE is designed to capture both local and global features of a graph by utilizing a deep neural network to transform node features and an encoder to process a graph's adjacency matrix. To ensure the encoded embeddings accurately represent the original manifold, we incorporate a reconstruction function. Furthermore, we propose a novel loss function, the manifold reconstruction loss, to enhance the quality of the embeddings. Experimental results demonstrate that UMCE outperforms existing state-of-the-art unsupervised graph embedding techniques on multiple datasets, showcasing its efficacy.

In the context of Grant-Free massive access, non-orthogonal multiple access is utilized to maximize spectral efficiency despite the absence of grant allocations. A key component of this approach involves designing sequences unique to each device, enabling simultaneous transmission. Nonetheless, the computational complexity of this process, specifically the optimization problem, hinders real-time implementation. To mitigate this issue, we propose a two-stage genetic algorithm that streamlines the optimization process, yielding suboptimal but effective results that match the performance of optimal scenarios in practical settings. The genetic algorithm's efficiency is further demonstrated by its ability to handle large problem dimensions with relative ease.

Combinatorial compressed sensing is concerned with determining an unknown k-element combinatorial set on an n-vertex graph from a small number of edge samples. This paper explores two scenarios: one in which the underlying graph structure is known and the other where it remains private. While the former scenario has been thoroughly researched, the latter has received limited attention. We introduce a novel algorithm, EC2, to address the latter scenario and demonstrate its ability to recover an accurate answer with high probability given a sufficient sample size, as defined by a specific formula, thus establishing a minimum sample requirement for recovery.

Domain shift poses significant challenges in supervised learning, where changes in the distribution of labels often hinder model performance. This issue is particularly problematic in semi-supervised learning, where limited labeled data and vast unlabeled data contribute to domain shift. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach that leverages adversarial domain representations for robust domain adaptation and generalization. This method involves two transformations: the adversarial transformation aligns label distributions across domains, whereas the stochastic transformation enhances model robustness. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on semi-supervised image classification tasks, where our method outperforms state-of-the-art models by providing robust generalization.

This paper demonstrates that for certain types of algebras, derivations that operate within two elements of the algebra are actually true derivations, which was previously proven for specific cases. We have expanded this concept to apply to more general algebras. Additionally, our research shows that derivations of certain algebras over unique ring systems can be entirely determined by the derivations of their sub-algebras, which can help clarify the properties of these derivations.

A specific type of singular point, referred to as a Dirac singularity in a phase space, is known to cause significant interference effects in quantum systems. Our research demonstrates that a geometric approach can effectively cancel out the singularity by introducing a small phase shift. Furthermore, we explore how the singularity behaves when viewed from a reference point in phase space, and we develop a method to calculate the wavefront pattern that emerges when this singularity occurs in a harmonic potential.

This study explores how spin-orbit interactions influence the formation of compactons in binary Bose-Einstein condates confined within harmonic potentials. We examine how the interplay between the spin-orbit coupling parameter $\lambda_{SO}$ and the magnetic field strength $\mathbf{b}$ impacts compacton formation. Additionally, we analyze the effect of non-magnetic mass variations within the condates on compacton characteristics.

The $\Lambda_c(2625)^+$ is seen as the massive quark spin symmetry counterpart to the $\Lambda_c(2595)^+$ in the context of quark content and spin-parity. It is suggested that the $\Lambda_c(2625)^+$ could be a $1/2^+$ state, consisting of a $u$, $c$ and $\bar{s}$ quarks, with the $\bar{s}c$ component mirroring that of the $\Lambda_c(2595)^+$ in terms of spin symmetry. The predicted mass of this state matches the experimental value, and its properties are further investigated in the context of the light-front quark-diquark model. The model's predictions for the decay of $\Lambda_c(2625)^+$ are also found to be in line with experimental observations.

Let G be a compact group, with X and Y being separable Banach spaces, and T be an operator that commutes with G. It's shown that for certain complex-valued functions f on the orbit space X/G, if both f and its conjugate, $\overline{f}$, are bounded on orbits under continuous one-parameter subgroups of G, then f is continuous on X/G. Furthermore, the range of f is compact in X/G if it's bounded on orbits. Additionally, the range of f being relatively weakly compact in the weak topology of L-infinity implies f's continuity on X/G.

Future high-energy muon colliders can serve as an optimal platform to detect axion-like particles, which have minimal interaction with the standard model and are potential candidates for new physics. These particles could contribute to the relaxation of the electroweak scale and act as a source of dark matter. Due to their light masses, ALPs can be generated in significant amounts through decays of heavy particles and can subsequently produce displaced vertices in the detector. The resulting signal can be amplified through the detection of secondary vertices separated by distances greater than a millimeter. The following white paper outlines the feasibility of such an experimental approach and the associated challenges.

The vast amount of data being transferred on modern networks has led to the need for more efficient network systems. To address this, cross-layer optimization holds great promise, especially with the advancement of open-source platforms that enable cross-layer coordination. However, implementing these optimizations in real-world scenarios is complicated by the numerous design choices involved. To facilitate comprehensive evaluations of cross-layer optimization platforms, we introduce MetaSys, an open-source framework that models and manages a wide range of network metadata, including network topology, data formats, and other relevant information. By leveraging this metadata, MetaSys enables the cross-layer coordination of applications, protocols, and network systems through cross-layer optimization algorithms and efficient resource utilization. To demonstrate MetaSys's capabilities, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of cross-layer optimizations in network applications, including data compression, network slicing, and edge computing, and show that these optimizations can significantly enhance system performance.

This research presents a new transfer learning approach, referred to as transfer with artificial data (TWA), which aims to address the limitations of traditional transfer learning in medical imaging. By utilizing Siamese networks, TWA enables the creation of artificial data that is tailored to a target domain, utilizing labels from that domain. This generated data is then combined with genuine data to train a neural network. Our experiments on two distinct medical imaging tasks, specifically skin lesion classification and brain tumor segmentation, demonstrate that TWA outperforms traditional transfer learning methods. Notably, TWA achieves results comparable to full-supervision on a publicly available dataset, while utilizing only 0.25% and 2.5% of the available labels, respectively.

We investigate a specific, bounded domain $\Omega\subset R^N$ and a related nonlinear elliptic system within it. The system, derived from the optimization of the energy functional, consists of two interconnected components - one focusing on the integral representation of the functional and the one-dimensional Sobolev exponent, and the other on the uniqueness of the system's both strong and weak solutions.

Neural networks struggle with learning long-term dependencies due to a problem known as the vanishing and exploding gradients problem. To overcome this, several state-of-the-art solutions have been proposed but these methods often sacrifice the ability to learn short-term relationships. To address this limitation, a new approach called the Fourier Recurrent Unit is proposed, which uses the Fourier transform to efficiently process long-term dependencies while maintaining the capability to learn short-term relationships. The proposed model outperforms existing solutions on multiple benchmarks and demonstrates superiority in handling long-term gradients. Additionally, it reduces the need for layer stacking, making it a more efficient solution.

This paper introduces a novel Markov decision process model and develops an algorithm to find the ideal policy within a finite time frame. The new model is based on a hidden-state hidden-action Markov decision process where both the state and action are partially known and the transition rule isn't accessible. In this setting, at each stage, the only information available is a vector composed of state, action, newly obtained reward, and a summary of previously taken actions. The agents within this framework operate under uncertainty, making this model applicable to real-world scenarios such as sensor networks, financial markets, and social interactions. The proposed algorithm utilizes a modified version of the Gittins policy, and demonstrates that it achieves the lowest possible regret, given a non-constant transition rule. The algorithm is further enhanced with a real-time adjustment mechanism to achieve the lowest possible regret even under a constant transition rule.

In this study, researchers propose a novel approach, dual-wake injection, to produce an extremely bright, short-lived and linearly polarized electron beam in the near extreme ultraviolet range, exceeding 100 kiloelectronvolts. This concept utilizes the plasma created from two intense, ultra-short laser pulses to inject two electron beams, which are then merged and focused into a single, highly concentrated beam. The authors present both theoretical and experimental findings from a setup using a linearly polarized near-Extreme Ultraviolet Laser Pulse, and an orthogonal, linearly polarized Petawatt Class Laser Pulse, that is set up to 10 degrees. The experiment successfully produced an electron beam with an energy of 140 kiloelectronvolts, an extremely low temporal spread of 140 femtoseconds, and an extremely high linearly polarized beam intensity of $5.5\times10^{20}$ W/cm$^2$/0.25% and a relatively low charge of 2.5 pC, thus achieving the desired ATtole electron beam. The researchers anticipate that this innovative approach will significantly contribute to the development of the ATtole electron Source.

Our world is predominantly populated by non-living, yet increasingly intricate, entities, whose level of complexity is hard to grasp. In contrast, living organisms have long been known to display complexity, prompting a search for a standard to gauge it. Observations in the realm of life have consistently shown that complexity is a driving force behind the universe's evolution. In this study, we introduce a universal, time-dependent metric called the Complexity Scale, which is a direct measure of the universe's overall complexity. By quantifying complexity, we can explore its development over time, shedding light on the universe's transition from a state of minimal to one of maximal complexity.

The effects of climate change are accelerating worldwide, with significant impacts on human health, the economy, ecosystems, and non-renewable resources. The climate crisis has become a global policy priority, prompting a surge in research and development activities focused on mitigating its causes and consequences. This study involves analyzing climate change research in the European Union using publicly accessible data from the Open Access repositories of 27 EU research funding organizations, specifically those of the Horizon2020 program. By applying the Sciencewise Focus Group's policy- relevant criteria, we identified over 100,000 research projects, which we then filtered using the INSPIREHEP and Climate Change Knowledge Portal classification systems to pinpoint 4,000 climate-related projects. This led to the development of a knowledge map illustrating climate research in the EU, which we used to discuss the benefits and limitations of using the web for policy support in the science-policy interface. Our analysis revealed that the majority of climate research focuses on its impacts and adaptation strategies, with significant interest in sea-level rise, while there is a notable gap in the study of climate-induced extreme events.

The most widely used mobile operating system, Android, is vulnerable to a particular type of cyber attack known as side-channel attacks. These threats can be used to extract sensitive information from applications. To combat this issue, this research introduces ASVAAN, a toolset designed to investigate the possibility of side-channel attacks in Android NDK applications. Through a comprehensive analysis of 10 side-channel vulnerabilities and 20 related attacks, ASVAAN provides a semi-automated method to assess the security of Android NDK applications. The research also identifies the challenges associated with evaluating side-channel vulnerabilities in this context.

Ethereum's growing popularity as a decentralized platform has led to an increase in on-chain transactions. Given the abundance of available transaction data, there's a pressing need to uncover the complex relationships within this information. This study delves into the properties of ego networks - a type of network that captures an individual account's transaction patterns over time - by labeling distinct accounts. Utilizing a substantial Ethereum dataset from 2018, our research examines temporal variations in ego networks' structural characteristics, highlighting differences between accounts with high and low transaction volumes.

The quantum fluctuations in a two-dimensional electron layer on the interface between LaAlO$_3$ and SrTiO$_3$ are examined, focusing on the effects of exposure to light. The study finds that the photo-induced increase in electronic density is primarily influenced by the energy of the absorbed light, whereas the shift in electronic band structure is linked to the intensity of the light. The results indicate that the optical processing of the 2D electron layer at the LAO/SrTiO$_3$ interface differs significantly from other semiconductor systems.

This paper explores the intricacies of the intrinsically dual nature of the pomset logic and von Neumann algebra framework. We prove duality for pomset logic and von Neumann algebra through a detailed analysis, demonstrating that dualities for pomset logic and its semantics and axiomatic structure are equivalent. We also investigate and compare the realisation of pomset logic and its semantics within different von Neumann algebra frameworks.
