To address this, we suggest introducing a blockchain that facilitates decentralized data storage and enables agents to collaborate and share information securely. Our approach incorporates a decentralized identification system, enabling agents to exchange information on a global scale while maintaining their anonymity, creating decentralized communities.

Our research focuses on the alpha-attractor model of inflation in both its standard and flat form, using a cosmological model with a flat metric. We calculate the power spectrum of curvature fluctuations under the slow-roll assumption, determining its amplitude and spectral index, ultimately obtaining the predicted inflationary scale. Forecasts reveal that future surveys will be able to constrain inflationary parameters with high precision, specifically predicting that NANOGrav and SKA will be able to constrain the spectral index with an accuracy of less than 0.01 and the amplitude to be less than 0.01. Furthermore, our analysis shows that combining data from CMB and surveys will allow us to distinguish between the alpha-attractor parameters with even higher precision.

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into diverse applications has become increasingly widespread. This has led to the expansion of pre-trained models into a wide array of new use cases, where they are fine-tuned to satisfy specific requirements. This process, known as a fine-tuned workflow, is gaining significant traction. A key factor in accelerating the adoption of fine-tuned workflows is the rising availability of pre-trained models. A major obstacle to the adoption of these models is the substantial data transfer time between the device generating the output and the AI engine processing the data. This paper presents strategies for optimizing the performance of fine-tuned workflows on Intel Xeon processors. A key innovation is the use of Xeon's AI-acceleration capabilities, including Intel Deep Learning Acceleration for CPUs (DLAC-MSI), to enhance performance. Additionally, the paper explores the utilization of Intel Xeon's offloading capabilities to accelerate AI workloads. These capabilities, which enable offloading to Intel Nervana Neural Stick (NNStk) on Xeon processors, are shown to provide substantial performance improvements. Ultimately, the performance benefits resulting from the combination of DLAC-MSI and NNStk enable end-to-end AI workflows to achieve performance comparable to that of specialized AI accelerators.

A novel Bayesian frequentist equivalence test, denoted as BF-ETF, is introduced and its relationship to the Bayes factor and ROPE-based equivalency tests is explored. It is demonstrated that BF-ETF can be precisely replicated from frequentist and Bayesian frameworks using the following equations: $z_{equ}=0$ and $BF_{ETF}=BF_{BF-ETF}$, where $z_{equ}$ represents the test statistic for frequentist and Bayes factor approaches, and $BF_{BF-ETF}$ is the Bayes factor for the hypothesis test. Furthermore, it is shown that the Bayes factor can be calculated from the equivalence test using the following equation: $BF_{BF-ETF}=\frac{1}{1+\exp\left(\frac{z_{equ}}{\sqrt{2}\text{se}}\right)}$, where $\text{se}$ represents the standard error associated with the test statistic. It is also shown that the Bayes factor can be calculated from the ROPE-based equivalency test using the following equation: $BF_{ROPE-ETF}=\frac{1}{1+\exp\left(\frac{z_{equ}}{\sqrt{2}\text{se}}\right)}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ for the frequentist approach and $\frac{1}{1+\exp\left(\frac{z_{equ}}{\sqrt{2}\text{se}}\right)}$

This research introduces a groundbreaking VQ-based transmission system that efficiently transmits images and their associated captions in vector form, facilitating the creation of a versatile image-caption combination system. Unlike conventional methods, our system is highly adaptable and can be seamlessly integrated with various image-caption combinations, such as those used in product image description, facial recognition, and augmented reality applications. The proposed system has a unique advantage in that it can generate novel image-captions combinations based on user-specified inputs. The generated captions serve as a means of customizing the image-caption combinations based on user preferences, and the accompanying image can be reconstructed using the generated caption vectors and the original image. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the system in terms of both efficiency and quality.

The rapid expansion of big data analytics is significantly impacting diverse sectors 
such as healthcare, finance, social media, and science, leading to a variety of 
opportunities and challenges. In this context, our research aims to explore the 
key elements required to deliver a comprehensive and user-friendly big data 
analytics platform. Notably, our work focuses on the development of an adaptive 
platform that personalizes the analytics experience based on user profiles. 
Additionally, we introduce an innovative framework that prioritizes the results 
of big data analytics. Through our approach, users can efficiently navigate the 
analytical process and quickly discover valuable insights. Ultimately, our research 
contributes to the advancement of Big Data Analytics by presenting a dynamic, 
interactive, and result-oriented solution.

A comonad is essentially the opposite concept to a monad; it is a structure consisting of three components - a mapping, a self-application mechanism, and an immersion - that functions inversely to a monad in the context of category theory. This paper introduces the fundamental principles and applications of comonads and provides an in-depth explanation of their role in functional programming. It also explores the connections between comonads and adjunctions and presents a range of relevant examples. Furthermore, the paper discusses the relationship between comonads and adjunctions and their interactions with the concept of monads. Additionally, the paper introduces the concept of enhancing a comonad with another comonad and demonstrates how this can be applied to the Eilenberg-Moore comonad.

A novel Bayesian nonparametric model is introduced to forecast time series data within interconnected networks that exhibit both temporal and clustering patterns. The Graphical Assistant Clustered Network Autoregression model (GACNAR) is comprised of a Dirichlet process-based clustering system and a hierarchical infinite mixture design. It categorizes network nodes into clusters based on their interdependencies and automatically creates a layered structure for modeling their time-series behavior. The model can be estimated using a hybrid of MCMC and expectation-maximization algorithms, with the latter serving to optimize the structure of the time-series models within the networks. A numerical study and an analysis of stock returns further demonstrate the model's effectiveness, followed by an examination of a large-scale network of GitHub repositories.

In the context of evidence retrieval and scientific claim verification, numerous studies have demonstrated that fine-tuning pre-trained language models on specific tasks enhances their performance.  However, fine-tuning these models significantly increases their size, making it challenging to utilize them in low-resource environments due to the requirement for large-scale computational capabilities.  Consequently, we investigate the feasibility of reducing the size of fine-tuned models through pruning and distillation, without compromising their performance.  Our experiments on two evidence retrieval datasets show that our approach can decrease the model size by 60-90% while preserving the performance of the original models.  Our findings indicate that these reduced model versions can be effectively utilized for scientific claim validation tasks.

The precise measurement of posterior segment (PS) thickness is a critical aspect of diagnosing ophthalmic and systemic diseases. This study introduces an innovative, automated system for estimating PS volume and thickness in 3D OCT scans, eliminating the need for manual labor. The proposed method, which employs a novel 3D Slicing-Separation-Resampling framework, surpasses conventional 2D approaches by accurately segmenting the PS in real-world OCT scans. The method was thoroughly evaluated using a comprehensive dataset of 420 OCT volumes and demonstrated exceptional accuracy, with high correlation coefficients and minimal differences in mean square error and root mean square deviation.

A substantial body of research has demonstrated that superstatistics effectively models complex systems by combining two different dynamical systems according to their operational conditions. We have developed a novel Bayesian neural network approach, called Neural Superstatistics, by utilizing a hierarchical probabilistic framework that identifies the presence of multiple dynamical systems within a given dataset. This proposed model allows us to identify the conditions that give rise to these distinct systems, as well as the conditions that lead to their transition. Our experiments on both artificial and real-world datasets have shown that this model outperforms traditional methods, including traditional machine learning and deep learning approaches, in accurately predicting dynamic changes in behavior. Furthermore, this model has been successfully applied to a well-known dataset in the cognitive neuroscience field, and the findings suggest that two distinct systems underlie math anxiety in college students, with system 1 activated under low conditions and system 2 activated under high conditions. This proposed model offers a new Bayesian framework for modeling and understanding dynamic changes in behavior, and its applications in the field of cognitive neuroscience hold significant potential.

This paper proposes a groundbreaking approach to uncovering Mersenne prime candidates. Notably, the proposed method has the ability to identify Mersenne prime numbers without relying on prior knowledge of their existence in a given period. Additionally, the proposed algorithm is straightforward and easy to implement. Moreover, the proposed method has a proven guarantee of accuracy, allowing it to directly pinpoint Mersenne prime numbers. Furthermore, the proposed method has a proven guarantee of optimality, indicating that it is not possible to devise a faster algorithm for this task. As a result, the proposed method outperforms existing expansion-based algorithms, such as the Binet formula, by being more efficient and capable of handling larger index ranges, thus making it more practical.

Hilbert posed six mathematical problems in 1907 and they significantly influenced the development of multiple fields. The sixth problem, which involves the generalization of a Taylor series expansion for all real values, especially for negative values, has considerable implications in mathematics and physics. The Taylor series expansion can be extended to approximate solutions of the Boltzmann and Euler equations, which are fundamental in modern physics and have significant implications in engineering. The correct Taylor coefficients can be determined through the hydrodynamic equations derived from the Boltzmann equation, and these can be extended to all fluid dynamics theories, including compressible and non-viscous systems. The research in this area has led to various applications, including the development of numerical methods, such as the DSMC and DSMC-DG methods, which involve the solution of the Euler and Navier-Stokes equations. The correct Taylor expansion coefficients can be used to validate the accuracy of these methods, and these can be extended to more complex systems, including the Navier-Stokes and Boussinesq equations, which involve higher-order terms. The research in this area has led to a better understanding of the behavior of complex systems, and it has also led to the development of more efficient numerical methods, which involve the solution of the Navier-Stokes and Boussinesq equations.

The presence of cold gas in galaxies is frequently examined using the fine structure transitions of neutral atomic hydrogen and carbon, however, research has demonstrated that these lines can be generated by lower-energy excitations. This phenomenon is particularly evident in the cores of nearby, star-forming galaxies, where simulations indicate that carbon line emissions originate from gas at significantly lower temperatures. Furthermore, it is discovered that the presence of cold gas in these galaxies can be effectively identified by analyzing the ratio of fine structure to non-fine structure line ratios. This study also explores the possibility of using these line ratios to determine the metallicity of galaxy cores.

Frisian is a low-level language spoken in the Netherlands, specifically in the northern part of the country, with limited resources available due to its unique historical status as a hybrid language of Dutch. This limited access to Frisian data poses a significant challenge for language learners, with only limited resources available in the language. This paper presents a novel approach to creating a treebank for spoken Frisian using transcribed data from spoken Dutch, with the aim of creating a shared language resource for native speakers and language learners. The paper provides an analysis of the challenges posed by the language's unique syntax and morphological features, with a focus on the verb-subject-unit (VSU) pattern, and outlines a set of conversion rules to create a treebank that accurately reflects the language's syntax, morphology, and phonology.

The process of photoevaporation is a crucial factor in the development of protoplanetary disks. Research suggests that it can be divided into two main phases, which are influenced by the disk's temperature and density. To understand how photoevaporation affects the dispersal of disks, simulations were conducted using the open-source code FARGO-3D. The study focused on how photoevaporation is affected by the mass of the star hosting the disk, as well as the disk's initial temperature and density. The results show that the dispersal of disks is significantly influenced by their stellar mass, particularly in the early stages of evolution. It was found that disks around more massive stars tend to be more resistant to dispersal, whereas those around lower mass stars are more easily affected. This difference in behavior can be attributed to the varying rates of photoevaporation in these systems. The initial temperature and density of disks also play a significant role in their dispersal, with disks having higher initial temperatures and densities being more resistant to dispersal. The study's findings have significant implications for understanding the development of protoplanetary disks and the formation of planets within these systems.

This study introduces a family of efficient time integration algorithms for dynamic structural analysis that can be easily incorporated into existing isogeometric analysis software using a straightforward substitution method. The proposed time integration schemes, which are based on the clear high-order $\alpha$ method, achieve stability without requiring a supplementary memory allocation, making them easy to implement. The proposed schemes are then tested through various numerical experiments on diverse types of problems including two-dimensional wave propagation and three-dimensional solid mechanics. The numerical results show that these new algorithms consistently outperform existing methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency, particularly when dealing with complex and challenging problems.

In this investigation, we analyze the decay rate of a Bose polariton, created when a single impurity interacts with a two-dimensional twin well containing an ultra-cold rubidium-87 gas, after the formation of a stable composite particle has been confirmed. The decay rate of the particle is measured by observing the rate at which its quasi-momentum distribution decays, and we find that this decay is influenced by the presence of certain inter-atomic interactions. The results of our study indicate that the observed decay is primarily caused by the transfer of energy from the particle to its surrounding bath through intra- and inter-band excitations, and our findings suggest that the decay rate is sensitive to the presence of these excitations at their resonant frequencies.

The conventional approach of using linear programming for logistics planning is no longer sufficient, especially in disaster relief situations where uncertainties are inherent and subject to constant changes. To address this limitation, a new framework is proposed, which integrates stochastic linear programming and simulation methods to create an adaptive and efficient logistics planning system. By combining these elements, the framework aims to minimize costs and meet demand under uncertain conditions. Initially, a linear programming model is developed to estimate the minimum required supply, considering both fixed and random demand within a set timeframe. To accommodate these uncertainties, a two-stage stochastic programming model is created, which takes into account multiple scenarios and solutions. To calculate scenario probabilities, a Markov chain model is used. To resolve the resulting complex mathematical problem, a multi-parametric quadratic programming model is used. To resolve the multiple scenarios in parallel, a multi-phase optimization technique is used. To resolve the large-scale linear programming model, a new adaptive algorithm is used. To resolve the global issue of uncertainty, a multi-parametric model is used. To resolve the uncertainty issue, a multi-phase optimization technique is used. To resolve the issue of uncertainty, a multi-parametric model is used. The proposed framework is demonstrated through a real-world case study. The results show that the proposed framework is effective in adapting to changes in the supply chain network, especially in disaster relief situations.

We investigate the timing array signal emitted by an elliptical binary system, focusing on its post-Newtonian corrections and their impact on precision and computational efficiency. Our calculations, conducted at Newtonian accuracy, yield a significant reduction in computational costs, amounting to a thousand times less time compared to a direct computation using post-Newtonian corrections. Notably, this advantage arises from the simplification of the signal's phase evolution, which relies on a single elliptical argument rather than multiple from each body. We also examine the significance of higher-order post-Newtonian corrections, finding that those beyond the first order have negligible effects in the context of timing array observations.

In this research, we examine the intricate relationships between players' actions and their movements within a global economy. We develop a comprehensive framework for analyzing the dynamic interplay between various agents' actions and their spatial locations, drawing on principles from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from from. This framework enables the identification of specific action patterns that emerge across diverse game scenarios. We also investigate the structural characteristics of these patterns and propose a method for creating a universal action language, which can be applied universally. Furthermore, we explore the potential for adaptive decision-making based on the actions of other players, specifically in auctions, and examine the underlying causes of the observed performance improvements.

A superconducting microwave resonator can accurately measure the absorption spectrum of molecular gases by analyzing the interaction between the device and the molecules. This technique, called cavity ring-down spectroscopy, offers high sensitivity and is particularly useful for detecting gases that are difficult to analyze through conventional methods. A superconducting microwave resonator was used to measure the absorption lines of formic acid, with results showing a good match to theoretical predictions across a range of frequencies. This study also found that the line shape of the absorption spectrum can be influenced by the sample's physical properties, providing valuable insights into the behavior of molecules in the terahertz range.

The COVID-19 pandemic has brought about a global health crisis, with far-reaching consequences that extend beyond health issues. Economic instability, social distancing measures, and increased anxiety have become widespread concerns. In an effort to combat this disease, a multi-faceted approach is necessary, combining both preventive and therapeutic measures. To address this challenge, our proposal is to develop a comprehensive artificial intelligence (AI) platform that provides a centralized tool for managing COVID-19, with the ultimate goal of accelerating the development of a cure. The platform will be designed to integrate various types of data, including clinical, social, and environmental information, to inform the creation of personalized vaccines and treatments tailored to specific patient profiles.

Interactions between multiple fluids and rigid or flexible structures are prevalent
in various fields, including the aerospace industry and biological systems. 
Predicting the behavior of these complex fluid-structure interactions is crucial.
In this paper, we introduce a multi-phase, multiple-fluid-structure interaction
framework grounded in the Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics method. This new framework
enables the modeling of complex, dynamic processes involving diverse fluid-structure
interactions. We validate the proposed model by simulating a specific scenario
involving a fluid and an elastic cylinder. This simulation shows promising results.

High-dimensional topological materials offer a unique, highly structured phase diagram that is driving cutting-edge research in topological systems. This complex topological landscape is characterized by the presence of topological nodal surfaces, which are becoming a focal point of topological materials research. This review delves into the topological features and invariances of these high-dimensional surfaces, while also highlighting recent breakthroughs in experimental realization of these surfaces in photonic materials. Additionally, it explores the broader implications of these surfaces, including their potential for implementation in other systems, such as matter-wave physics and various quantum materials.

The LHCC identified and approved several Physics TDRs, including Top Quark, Higgs Boson, and Exotic Physics TDRs, to assess the HL-LHC's simulation and reconstruction needs. In response to these demands, the Large Hadron Collider Computing Community Facility (LHCcc) and CMS have initiated shared software projects for Monte Carlo generation and simulation. CMS has selected and is evaluating two event generators: Herwig7 and Sherpa, with the aim of selecting one for HL-upgrade simulations. In contrast, the LHCcc has initiated the Pythia 8 project. This document outlines the current status of event generators, future development plans, and long-term simulation and reconstruction strategies.

The paper examines certain types of means, such as arithmetic, geometric, and harmonic means, in the context of spaces with positive definite metrics. It provides definitions and characteristics of means in normed and semi-definite spaces, and identifies specific examples of means in these spaces. Furthermore, the geometric and harmonic means are shown to exhibit invariant characteristics in semi-definite spaces. To prove this, the concept of invariant characteristics of means is extended to semi-definite spaces. Additionally, the geometric and harmonic means are shown to be invariant under endomorphisms in semi-definite spaces. As a result, the existing theorem of Karamata is generalized to the semi-definite space setting.

The formation of stars above $10,000$ per year in the TeV gamma-ray source NGC 7027 is thought to be facilitated by a disk of dense, turbulent gas located beyond the source's central shock region. This outer disk likely extends beyond its observed size, with a mass exceeding $0.1$ solar masses. This study presents high-resolution observations of the $13$CO($J = 1 \to 0$) line emission in the outer region of the source, which reveals a $2.5$ parsec diameter disk with a mass of approximately $0.5$ solar masses. This outer disk is composed of $20\%$ dense gas with a density of $10^{5}$ cm$^{-3}$, which is connected to the source's central shock region through a low-density outflow. This outflow's energy is likely generated from the source's central shock region and is responsible for transporting material and energy away from the source's central area. This study's findings are the first to provide observational evidence for the source's dark disk's connection to its central shock region.

In a closed economy, the labor market is analyzed to assess how different cost components affect the wage structure. An important aspect of this analysis is the impact of the law of one price on wage movements when there is variation in the non-labor cost factors among different firms. The proposed wage theory has potential implications in both developed and developing economies, particularly in situations where firms in the low-wage sector have more flexibility to set prices.

Our research involves analyzing the mechanical response of an active gel with polar components. Owing to the diversity of biological tissues, this system holds great potential for gaining insights into the mechanical properties of various tissues, including the liver, bone, and intervertebral discs. By employing coarse-graining and treating each polar particle as a polar, anisometric elastic sphere, we have developed a model that captures the behavior of these particles in the mesoscale. Our findings reveal that active polar gels exhibit distinct properties compared to passive, polar gels, including a higher storage modulus and a more pronounced shear modulus. Furthermore, we observe a transition from solid-like behavior to fluid-like behavior as the activity level is increased. Additionally, we identify a unique collective motion within the active polar gel, characterized by the rotation of polar particles in the plane perpendicular to their polar axis, which is influenced by the nematic order.

Within the framework of quark Bag model, we investigate the doubly charmed baryon state spectrum and the semileptonic interactions $D^*(0)_c 	o D^*(0)_c \ell 
u_\ell$ where $\ell = \mu, 	au$. Our findings indicate that the mass of the $D^*(0)_{cc}$ pentaquark is approximately 3.6 GeV, and the state is non-singlet. We discovered that the matrix elements $f_{V_1}$ and $f_{P_1}$ related to the first type of semileptonic decay are significantly larger than the corresponding matrix elements $f_{V_2}$ and $f_{P_2}$ associated with the second type of semileptonic decay. Additionally, we observed that the branching ratio for the undecayed state $B_c 	o D_s^+ \mu^+ 
u_\mu$ is approximately 0.01, and the branching ratios for the decays $B_c 	o D_s^+ \mu^+ 
u_\mu$ and $B_c 	o D_s^+ 	au^+ 
u_	au$ are $0.01$ and $0.05$ respectively.

This research introduces the Where Are You? task, a groundbreaking task in embodied dialogue that focuses on locating a query target in a given environment through spoken communication. In this task, a communicator attempts to pinpoint the location of a query target via conversation, using only visual data to guide the discussion. We present a large dataset of this task, created from the Google Landmark Training Set and an initial model that demonstrates its capabilities. This work also explores the task through the lens of value-based reinforcement learning, where the learning process is divided into two stages: the first stage is to develop a visual understanding of the environment, and the second stage is to leverage this understanding in the dialogue for more efficient location.

This research introduces a novel frequency band selection technique tailored for vibration analysis of rotating machinery that is resilient against noise and data imperfections. The Band Importance Factor (BIF) prioritizes frequency bands with high relevance scores while disregarding less significant ones. The proposed BIF method relies on a novel importance factor-based index that leverages the top three singular values of a vibration signal's autocorrelation matrix. The index is then normalized to yield a metric known as the importance factor ratio (IFR), which is used to evaluate the importance of specific frequency bands. The BIF method is tested on simulated and real-world data sets from various machines, including a single-motor test, a cooling fan, and an industrial gas turbine, demonstrating the technique's effectiveness in band selection.

Our investigation into the CaTiSi3 and CaPtSi3 noncentrosymmetric superconductors utilized both temperature-dependent zero-field muon spin spectroscopy and magnetic-field-induced muon spin resonance techniques. These experiments, which measured muon spin relaxation and muon spin rotation, revealed that CaTiSi3 and CaPtSi3 exhibit typical type-II superconductivity behavior. Notably, the analysis of the field-dependent muon spin relaxation data in CaTiSi3 and CaPtSi3 suggested a lower upper critical field at 3 Tesla for CaPtSi3 compared to CaTiSi3. Furthermore, the temperature dependence of the muon spin relaxation line shape indicated that both superconductors exhibit strong electron-phonon coupling. These findings are corroborated by an extended s-wave superconducting state, as evidenced by the muon spin relaxation and rotation data.

We introduce the Sparse Grid Feedback Mitigation (SGFBM) algorithm, a numerical solution for the continuous-time Feedback Linearization problem. Unlike traditional methods, SGFBM uses the sparse grid method to efficiently tackle high-dimensional nonlinear equations and optimal control issues. By applying SGFBM to three-dimensional problems, it achieves a significant computational advantage, outperforming existing methods by several orders of magnitude. Additionally, its high-accuracy results make SGFBM a viable alternative in practical applications.

Classifying high-dimensional data in machine learning is a difficult task, particularly when the data points are from a complex quantum space that doesn't work well with traditional algorithms. To address this challenge, our research focuses on a specific classification problem known as quantum evaluation classification, which involves labeling high-dimensional features rather than just binary classification. We have developed an efficient new method that uses a single layer of neural network operation to project the data into a lower dimensional space that is suitable for classification, thereby avoiding the curse of dimensionality. We have tested this approach on both classical and quantum data sets and our method outperforms existing algorithms, particularly on high-dimensional quantum data.

The goal of the European Union's Energy Transition is to achieve nearly carbon-neutral electricity generation by 2035, yet this objective is hindered by the established infrastructure, leading to an increase in the use of fossil fuels for heating and transportation. To mitigate climate change, researchers are proposing innovative solutions such as electro-thermal heating, utilizing heat pumps and smart grids, and novel transportation methods like electric and hydrogen-powered vehicles. These technologies, although existing for a long time, have a significant impact when combined in dynamic energy systems. This study presents a comprehensive modeling framework for multi-energy dynamical systems (MEDS) that incorporates various energy vectors, sectors, and innovative technologies, and develops a control strategy to address existing and future challenges. Through a case study, the authors demonstrate that the proposed MEDS model can effectively capture the dynamics of sector-coupled energy systems and that the control strategy can be used to achieve a carbon-neutral energy system by 2035, even with existing infrastructure.

The 2D filtration model is a fundamental concept in many research areas, including physics, engineering, and biology. It has numerous practical applications across various fields. This paper presents a novel approach to developing a general model for two-dimensional particle or fluid flow through a porous medium. This model integrates concepts from physics of engineering and biology, thereby eliminating their individual limitations. This paper also introduces a method for automating the process of solving the 3D and 2D filtration model using machine intelligence. It utilizes genetic algorithms to optimize the model's parameters. This paper further demonstrates the utility of the 2D filtration model in two distinct scenarios. Firstly, it illustrates the significant discrepancies that can arise between three-dimensional and two-dimensional flow predictions. Secondly, it illustrates the applicability of the 2D model to very different systems, including biological systems, traditional porous media, and even non-porous media.

Utilizing rapid MRI to monitor the thermal dissipation in a stationary bed of glass particles heated by a CO2 laser, which induces a non-uniform temperature gradient, is demonstrated. A mathematical model is then developed to describe the thermal conduction in the bed system, taking into account the heat transfer through the particles and gas, and the effects of radiation. This model is validated using experimental data obtained from MRI temperature measurements across various laser beam positions and width adjustments, which also enable the calculation of the thermal diffusivity value.

In the compound UTe$_2$, reentrant superconductivity has been observed under high pressure and the role of magnetically active electrons is investigated. A theoretical model is developed to explain superconductivity in the presence of magnetically active electrons, incorporating a dynamic exchange field, which leads to the formation of a composite order parameter. This composite order parameter is composed of two distinct components: a Cooper pair-mediated pair correlation function and a dynamic exchange field-induced pair correlation function. Our analysis shows that the dynamic exchange field, influenced by temperature and wave-vector properties, significantly affects the superconducting behavior, leading to the emergence of reentrant superconductivity. At low temperatures, the composite order parameter exhibits a complex behavior, with two distinct minima, which is attributed to the competition between the dynamic exchange field and the pair correlation function. This competition leads to the enhancement of superconductivity at temperatures higher than the critical temperature of the Cooper pair. Furthermore, the application of an external magnetic field is found to suppress the superconducting behavior, which is in line with the experimental observations of the compound UTe$_2$.

Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) is a highly effective method for addressing issues in wireless communication systems. In this context, we apply DRL to adjust the radio settings of ultra-wideband communication devices in real-time. Our goal is to minimize the overall error rate by fine-tuning parameters such as symbol duration, preamble code length, and packet length. Utilizing deep reinforcement learning, we demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms traditional fixed settings.

We examine the $k$-median clustering problem in metric spaces, particularly focusing on two key metrics: the Frechet distance and the Hausdorff distance, both in a finite set of points. By considering the minimum sum of distances between pairs of points, we establish that the $k$-median clustering problem remains NP-hard under both distance measures. However, we also show that the problem becomes fixed-parameter tractable when combined with the number of clusters $k$. Moreover, we establish that the problem can be efficiently solved in practice when the input points are small in size, particularly through a randomized algorithm that runs the linear time when the input points are small in size.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) methods based on policy iteration are often paired with optimization techniques, such as Q-learning and its variants. However, these single-step approaches can be inefficient and prone to instability issues. To address this, we explore the use of dual averaging in a primal-dual framework for policy iteration-based MARL, yielding several positive outcomes. Firstly, we derive a policy iteration algorithm that achieves the best possible regret within a fixed timeframe in both fully and partially observed environments. Secondly, we develop a MARL algorithm based on linear programming that converges rapidly to a Nash equilibrium. To improve the algorithm's performance, we introduce a regularization scheme to introduce slack in the constraints, resulting in a dual update rule with a novel form. Finally, we demonstrate the algorithm's efficiency in solving the cooperative mountain-car problem.

This paper presents a coalgebraic method for proving that arithmetic $\mu$-calculi meet their termination criteria, thereby establishing soundness of their closed types systems to verify program satisfaction of decidable first-order logic formulas without the need for explicit encoding. The method's effectiveness is confirmed through its successful application to verify the soundness of Coq's $\mu$CPS translation of Wasm.

Sparse initial values in many partial differential equations are known to lead to sparsity and accelerated convergence rates in solution processes.  However, accurately determining these initial values often requires significant amounts of data and computational resources.  This paper proposes a novel method to address this challenge, which involves representing the initial values as reduced-rank multi-way tensors, and provides a theoretical framework for their sparse structure.  Furthermore, the paper introduces a non-convex optimization algorithm to recover these sparse initial values, and demonstrates its effectiveness in both low and high-dimensional isogeometric settings for a hyperbolic equation.

This research introduces an innovative approach to creating detailed air conditioning map models, which are essential for navigation systems in urban areas. Traditional map creation methods rely heavily on expensive and labor-intensive processes such as mapping GPS to AC unit outputs. In contrast, our novel method leverages information collected from AC facilities through 'driven by sensing', a technique that tracks the movement of units. Our proposed method, which focuses on high-resolution AC map creation, enables the creation of maps based solely on sensor data. A key component is a regression model that accurately predicts the location of each AC facility using the collected sensor information. Additionally, our approach includes a novel clustering algorithm that accounts for the varying speeds of AC facilities to generate accurate map boundaries. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our method, achieving an accuracy rate of 80% in localizing AC facilities and a map accuracy rate of 60-80% in terms of drive path accuracy.

This study aims to develop a Weil representation for the generalized special linear group, which is defined over a domain comprised of reduced integer parts of complex numbers with a second class involution, in association with a finite field. The associated quadratic form is then used to construct the Weil representation for the generalized linear group, which is derived from the group of rings used previously. The research also involves investigating the Weil representation for the generalized special linear group, which is defined over a domain comprising reduced integer parts of complex numbers with a second class involution, utilizing a specific basis.

Artificially generated videos are now being produced using advanced deep learning technology, which can be manipulated to convey false information. As a result, there is a pressing need to develop approaches that can automatically identify and reject fake videos and create realistic ones that are difficult to detect. This research paper undertakes a comprehensive analysis of the challenges and opportunities associated with artificially creating videos that are convincing. The study categorizes and examines various approaches to evaluate and create convincing videos, including the underlying architectures used. The study also identifies key issues and proposes potential research directions in this area.

A novel approach to minimize the required storage of quantum information in quantum systems involves compressing data using a more compact representation. This concept, known as compressed coherent states, has been successfully demonstrated in various quantum systems, including atomic and optical systems. This study explores the application of compressed coherent states to ions confined within an ion trap, which is a fundamental component in quantum computing technology. We present a theoretical framework for applying this principle to ions in both quadrupole and hexapole ion traps, and we identify the key parameters that influence the behavior of these systems. Our findings suggest that the use of compressed coherent states in ion traps could lead to more efficient and scalable quantum computing technology.

The complexity of simulating biological systems is a pressing issue in neuroscience research, where the development of reliable models is crucial for accurately predicting and replicating findings. However, the creation of such models involves a substantial investment of time and resources, primarily due to the extensive computational requirements necessary to validate and analyze them. In an effort to alleviate this problem, we propose an innovative framework centered on the Learning to Learn concept, which enables the automated optimization of model-specific parameters via self-adaptive learning methods. Our proposed system is designed to operate in conjunction with existing models and leverage the capabilities of high-performance computing systems to optimize model accuracy in response to varied input stimuli. In this study, we present the results of our framework's application to the NEST model of the rat whisker system, ultimately leading to the discovery of an optimal parameter configuration that successfully replicates the experimental findings.

The task of hiding objects within images to make them undetectable to computer vision systems has gained significant attention recently. In contrast, this work instead focuses on concealing instances within images using adversarial attacks and then develops techniques to reveal the concealed objects. We introduce a new dataset featuring in-the-wild natural images with instances concealed through adversarial attacks. This dataset is designed to test the robustness of computer vision systems in real-world scenarios. We also develop a context-based segmentation approach that leverages the original image context to uncover the concealed instances. Moreover, we establish a benchmark suite for assessing the real-world vulnerability of various computer vision systems. Comprehensive experiments are conducted to evaluate the performance of different methods in concealing and revealing instances.

In the context of superconductivity, we explore the effects of Lorentz invariance breaking, focusing on scenarios where a preferred frame exists. We consider a Lagrangian density that incorporates Lorentz breaking terms, influencing the Cooper factor and superconducting condensate. The resulting BCS gap can exhibit chiral symmetry under specific conditions, while the superconducting phase possesses topological characteristics in certain cases. Notably, the BCS gap can reach the speed of light or exceed it, depending on whether the electromagnetic interaction is mediated by photons or massive photons.

As AI systems become increasingly prevalent, it is crucial to have a thorough grasp of their reliability. Our method involves gathering reports from individuals who have encountered errors in AI systems and utilizing these reports to identify issues that may have previously gone unnotified. Our approach involves a two-stage process: first, we analyze the reports to pinpoint the input parameters that may contribute to an error; second, we utilize this insight to conduct targeted tests of the AI system, focusing on the identified parameters. Our method was successfully tested on a range of visual AI models, including a model designed to detect objects and another for image classification. Our analysis revealed that individuals who participated in our study were able to identify multiple errors in the AI systems that had previously gone unnotified. Our method also enabled us to verify that these errors were indeed legitimate issues. Furthermore, our method was able to identify errors in the AI models that had not been previously documented. Our results demonstrate the potential of leveraging crowd-sourced information to uncover errors in complex AI models.

Object detection in images is a complex task, requiring the simultaneous prediction of various variables such as object locations, sizes, shapes, and classifications. Conventional approaches typically rely on a straightforward sequential process, often incorporating a single-stage processing network that prioritizes one type of variable over the others, resulting in a trade-off between performance and accuracy. In contrast, our proposed method, R(Det)^2, offers a novel stochastic decision routing mechanism that enables the model to adaptively choose between focusing on object locations, sizes, shapes, and classifications at both low and high resolution levels, thereby streamlining the training process and enhancing overall accuracy. Through comprehensive experiments on the MS-COCO benchmark, R(Det)^2 has demonstrated superior performance compared to existing methods, achieving state-of-the-art results with a ResNet-50 backbone and a mAP of 41.0%, and similarly outperforming other state-of-the-art approaches with a mAP of 38.2% using a ResNet-18 backbone. The corresponding source code will be made publicly available.

To enhance model resilience against adversarial attacks, adversarial training involves training with intentionally generated adversarial examples. However, this process often results in a significant decline in model performance on standard test data. This paper presents ZeroGrad, an improved adversarial training approach based on FGSM, that not only reduces performance losses on standard test data but also provides greater defense against FGSM attacks. Our analysis indicates that FGSM-based adversarial training often leads to substantial overfitting due to FGSM gradient magnification, a phenomenon where the FGSM gradient of the cross-entropy loss concerning model parameters exceeds that of the clean data gradient. This phenomenon causes rapid model degradation. By employing FGSM on both standard and mixed clean data, ZeroGrad mitigates overfitting and enhances test data accuracy. Our experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-1K show that ZeroGrad achieves a 50\% reduction in performance loss on standard test data and a 10\% decrease in FGSM attack accuracy compared to vanilla FGSM-based adversarial training.

Recent research on the Thakurta metric, a hypothetical form of black hole metric resulting from a specific type of star formation process, has led to claims that it may be distinguishable from the standard Schwarzschild metric in gravitational wave observations. This assertion relies on the assumption that the Thakurta metric is identical to the metric of cosmological black holes. We demonstrate that this assumption is invalid and show that the Thakurta metric does not accurately describe the geometry of cosmological black holes. Consequently, the Thakurta metric's unique features are not observable, and our findings indicate that the Thakurta metric is not distinguishable from the Schwarzschild metric, including the Thakurta metric's parameter range that can be used to describe the properties of cosmological black holes.

This research paper investigates the effects of non-continuous variable values on algorithms that use a variant of the Markov Chain Monte Carlo choice of sampling centers. Specifically, it investigates the performance of the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) and the Nuts Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HNuts) including its three variations: HNuts-DG, HNuts-SL, and HNuts-HC. By running the research in parallel on a GPU, the study analyzes the performance of these algorithms in comparison to a baseline created by adjusting the non-continuous variable values in the data. The research also compares the performance of these algorithms to a baseline created by adjusting the non-continuous variable values in the data. The results of this research were based on a variety of machine learning tasks, such as regression, classification, and density estimation, across multiple probability distributions.

A fully homomorphic encryption scheme allows data to be processed in the cloud without decrypting it, giving users complete control over data accessibility. However, current FHE implementations face significant hurdles in terms of performance. To overcome this limitation, we focus on bootstrappability as a key requirement for large-scale FHE adoption. In this paper, we present an innovative bootstrapping approach for FHE that significantly enhances data encryption efficiency. This approach leverages a novel method of data homomorphism to eliminate the need for costly re-encryption. Theoretical analysis and experimental data confirm the substantial benefits of our proposed bootstrapping technique, showcasing promising results in terms of both speed and security.

This paper delves into various aspects of random matrix collections, focusing on the behavior of logarithmic confining potentials. We establish the existence of steady-state configurations and analyze how these systems evolve over time. By approximating the energy distribution within these collections, we provide insight into their structural organization. Furthermore, we examine the impact of varying interaction potentials within these collections and demonstrate how the confining potential significantly influences the dynamics of these systems. The outcomes of this study contribute to a broader understanding of random matrix collections.

Our experiments have successfully demonstrated the existence of quantum connections within the two-qutrit Hilbert space of a NV center NVR. By tracking the evolution of entanglement between the center of mass and the spin degrees of freedom of the NV center's spin state, we confirmed the predicted relationship. Furthermore, we observed the disappearance of quantum connections when the driving force is eliminated, indicating that these connections rely on the applied classical field. Our research on the NVR system has provided valuable insights into the mechanisms behind the emergence of quantum connections, contributing to a deeper understanding of the underlying principles. This knowledge may ultimately lead to the development of quantum technologies such as quantum sensors and quantum-based machine learning algorithms.

In the context of Bell's theorem, we explore the implications of decomposable biseparable states, examining how state decomposition influences the inequality. The relationship between state decomposability and local hidden variables is analyzed, along with a discussion on whether this connection can address the Bell inequality violation. Additionally, we consider the trade-off between state decomposability and the extent of the observers' spatial separation as they attempt to achieve a Bell inequality violation.

We introduce StyleGAN-V, a versatile tool for creating high-quality videos using various formats. Built on the solid foundation of StyleGAN-V1, StyleGAN-V offers significant improvements in video quality, while achieving this through minor adjustments to the architecture, requiring minimal changes to the training process. Notably, StyleGAN-V operates at a computational expense comparable to StyleGAN-2, making it an efficient solution for video generation. One notable aspect of StyleGAN-V lies in its capacity to seamlessly switch between video resolutions and frame rates without necessitating retraining, much like StyleGAN-2 when switching between image resolutions. To illustrate StyleGAN-V's versatility, we showcase its application in various video generation tasks, including video super-resolution, video deblurring, and the creation of 60fps videos from 30fps ones.

We explore the differences in degrees associated with the etale correspondences across various fields. Our research contributes the initial numerical formula for degree discrepancies across the etale correspondence on a curve over a finite field with characteristic zero and establishes analogous findings for pseudo-Hom and pseudo-Ind correspondences. Furthermore, we derive a novel calculation of the degree discrepancy in degree zero for the full etale correspondence on a curve and provide a detailed account of its interactions with degree discrepancies observed in p-adic etale correspondences by Ellenberg, Erman, and Preiss.

The primary technique for radiation dose assessment in medical dosimetry is
primarily based on thermoluminescence (TL) detection. Although TL dosimetry is
generally precise, its application is often hindered by background noise and
interference from radiation sources. Consequently, TL signal intensity is
substantially reduced, making it difficult to accurately determine exposure
dates. In this study, we utilize a deep learning model to overcome this
limitation. The model was trained using simulated TL dosimetry data and was
evaluated based on its ability to accurately estimate dose and exposure dates.
The results demonstrated that the model can achieve high levels of accuracy even
at extremely low signal-to-noise ratios. The study highlights the potential of
deep learning to revolutionize TL dosimetry by allowing for the estimation of
dose and exposure dates from low-intensity TL signals.

We explore the existence and nonexistence of nontrivial solutions for a singular, perturbed nonlinear problem in a complete manifold. This problem is characterized by a lower order, nonlinear operator with variable exponent and nonlinearity that exhibits singular behavior at the manifold's boundary, causing a loss of regularity. To address this lower order, we employ Sobolev spaces within the context of variable exponents and demonstrate that solutions can be found through a fixed point analysis, utilizing the Banach fixed point theorem, provided that the Sobolev exponent meets certain conditions and the nonlinear operator's growth does not exceed a certain rate.

Fastcat cone beam CT (CBCT) systems, installed in radiation therapy machines, provide real-time tomographic images. This feature is particularly beneficial for treating head and neck cancers, as it's challenging to align cervical and head cancers with precision using radiation therapy. CBCT images aid in patient setup and enable the correction of positioning errors. This study involved developing and validating a software tool that generates realistic CBCT images based on radiation therapy cone shapes and beam characteristics. Cone profiles were created using a mathematical model, and the tool was tested using actual cone beam CT images. Our findings show that the simulator can produce accurate images when specific parameters are set correctly. This tool has the potential to simplify the process of CBCT image correction in radiation therapy machines, reducing the complexity of the process.

Machine learning model interpretation has gained significant attention, with feature attribution techniques being particularly popular. Notable methods include SHAP and LIME, which utilize perturbation and regression. However, these techniques can be unstable due to the nature of the task and the methods used, leading to inconsistent attributions. To address this, we have developed a novel approach called S-LIME, which incorporates stabilization through smoothness constraints to provide more reliable feature attributions. S-LIME achieves this by adding a smoothness penalty to the optimization problem, ensuring that feature attributions are consistent and stable. Our experiments demonstrate that S-LIME produces more reliable attributions compared to other methods, and our code is available for public use.

In machine learning, particularly in computer vision and natural language processing, accurate classification is a key objective, but there is a growing recognition of the limitations of solely providing classification results. There is a pressing need to develop more effective approaches for classifying inputs and justifying the confidence levels associated with these classifications. This study proposes a novel Bayesian framework that not only classifies inputs, but also provides a justification for each classification, using a model of the input's true label. By incorporating feedback from the user, this framework can refine its model and improve the accuracy of future classifications. In an experiment using a text classification task, we demonstrate that our approach can enhance the user's classification abilities and achieve better results than traditional classification methods.

TbInO$_3$ is an intriguing spin-liquid candidate with a unique double-helix crystal structure that sets it apart from its Ce and Yb counterparts. Despite its potential for interesting physics, the magnetic properties of triangular-lattice TbInO$_3$ remain poorly understood. To better comprehend its behavior, researchers must first understand the impact of crystal-field and spin-orbit interactions on its magnetic ions. To this end, the study employs advanced spectroscopic techniques such as terahertz and mid-infrared light to create a detailed map of TbInO$_3$'s crystal-field excitations. By analyzing these data and combining it with theoretical simulations, researchers were able to create a detailed, accurate model of the compound's electronic and vibrational properties, including the detailed patterns of its spin states and the specific vibrations of its two distinct crystallographic sites. This groundbreaking research paves the way for further investigation into the unusual properties of triangular-lattice spin-liquid systems.
We demonstrate the existence and stability of a unique self-similar solution to the convex mean curvature flow in higher dimensional space.

A new technique for quickly and efficiently learning shallow neural networks is introduced, utilizing the network's structure in the spectrum domain. By applying this innovative approach, it becomes possible to achieve high performance with smaller network sizes, resulting in substantial reductions in computational requirements. Initially developed for image processing tasks, this method can also be adapted for use in signal processing applications. Additionally, it has been mathematically proven that this technique will consistently produce networks with reduced complexity, regardless of the underlying data distribution.

The primary goal of image grouping is to segment an image into clusters of coherent texture, which is crucial for tasks such as object segmentation and image compression. Although significant progress has been made in image grouping, existing deep learning models still struggle with accurately segmenting images with complex structures. To address this challenge, we introduce a new ensemble learning approach that leverages the strengths of multiple deep neural networks. Our proposed technique, DeepCluE, is a multi-layer ensemble model that combines the outputs of individual networks at various stages. We also introduce a novel clustering objective function that incorporates a combination of local and non-local texton affinity matrices. Our experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of DeepCluE, with our model outperforming the state-of-the-art by achieving a maximum F-score of 0.7324 on the KITTI image dataset.

Organizational risk detection involves identifying potential risks and their connections to assets through a structured approach. However, traditional methods in this field are limited as they fail to account for the dynamic nature of risks and the extensive information involved. To address these shortcomings, we present an innovative framework that utilizes knowledge graphs to effectively store and analyze vast risk data. By integrating this system with real-time social media and media monitoring tools, our framework can provide continuous updates on changing risks. Through actual implementation and testing, we demonstrate that our proposed solution surpasses existing commercial solutions in risk detection and information retrieval tasks.

Data categorization, a pivotal process in machine learning, receives considerable attention due to its importance. This research contributes a new method for categorization that leverages topological characteristics of data to create classes. By combining the Siamese Neural Network with the Betti numbers of its manifold, which are determined by the data's Siamese input pairs, this method offers a way to define classes that are natural to the intrinsic data structure. The presented method's effectiveness was evaluated on the MNIST, CIFAR-10, and W-MNIST datasets, with notable success in transferring knowledge to an unfamiliar dataset (W-MNIST).

A well-established similarity metric known as contrasimilarity has been used to measure semantic similarity between basic program constructs.  The similarity between two constructs can be calculated by simulating a game-based comparison between the two.  Each construct is represented as a strategy that determines the outcome of comparing two terms within a specific programming context.  The similarity between two constructs is then determined by the probability of success in simulating one construct against the other in different possible scenarios.  However, a concern has been raised about the accuracy of this approach, particularly in certain types of programming that involve comparing values for the purpose of determining equality.  An alternative game-based approach has been proposed, but the new metric does not produce the same results as the original metric in all cases.  The main goal of this research is to establish a game description for the original metric that is compatible with the alternative metric under certain conditions of equality assessment.

The string 2-group, denoted as string group 2-group, represents a fundamental concept in string theory that serves as the string group. This group functions as the gauge group of closed strings and plays a pivotal role in the string group's properties, including its universal string group. The string group has far-reaching implications in string theory, encompassing its cohomology, classification, and behavior under string group conjugation. Notably, the string group also underlies the string group's universal covering group. This discussion will delve into the string group's inherent properties, beginning with its initial identification and examination of its category-based representation.

Numerical simulations have been conducted to investigate the formation of ion-acoustic rogue waves in a double pair plasma system consisting of non-extensive particles. This system features stationary, positively and negatively charged ions and non-extensive electrons. Using a quasi-static, non-linear perturbation method to derive a modified Korteweg-de Vries equation, the nonlinear evolution of small-amplitude waves was analyzed. The results showed that ion-acoustic waves in non-extensive electrons can be compressed due to their negative non-extensivity parameter, resulting in the formation of higher amplitude waves and rogue waves. The nonlinear evolution of these rogue waves was observed to result in the formation of shock waves, which can give rise to rogue waves. The influence of non-extensivity parameters on the formation of these rogue waves was found to be significant, with electron non-extensivity having a greater impact than ion non-extensivity.

A novel approach to modeling the Alfv\'en wave parametric decay instability in a low-temperature plasma has been developed, incorporating both kinetic theory and fluid modeling. This hybrid model replicates the energy transfer between the unstable Alfv\'en wave and the plasma's microinstabilities, accurately capturing the number density evolution. When compared to linear fluid models, it has been found that the inclusion of a kinetic component enhances the instability's growth rate. This enhancement is most significant when the unstable wave closely matches both the unstable ion-Alfv\'en wave and unstable ion-sound wave frequencies.

We investigate the impact of ambipolar diffusion on the gravitational instability of a thin, cylindrical molecular cloud. This cloud, comprising an isothermal gas with magnetic fields parallel to its axis, is subject to a uniform gravitational field. As the ambipolar diffusion of magnetic fields disrupts the magnetic flux conservation, the cloud undergoes slow diffusion along its axis. In response, the cloud expands and its magnetic field becomes increasingly tilted. Consequently, the cloud's stability is significantly altered. Initially, an increase in ambipolar diffusion rate leads to a reduction in the cloud's stability, causing a sharp decrease in the shortest wavelength mode's growth rate as the cloud's expansion velocity increases. However, once the cloud's expansion velocity reaches a specific velocity, the growth rate rapidly increases, leading to a cloud with a critical ambipolar diffusion rate. This critical rate is directly related to the cloud's aspect ratio and is independent of its initial size. This research provides a starting point for understanding the filamentary structure of molecular clouds, including those in which magnetic fields play a significant role.

The impact of frequent measurements on the evolution of a quantum system is still a topic of discussion, with the Zeno and anti-Zeno effects being observed and explained in the weak coupling scenario. This research aims to extend our understanding of these phenomena in the case of strong coupling between the system and its environment. This challenge arises due to the influence of the environment on the system's evolution, as monitoring it becomes difficult in the strong coupling regime. To address this, we have developed a new theoretical model that can describe the effects of frequent measurements on the system's evolution in the strong coupling regime. This model is based on the concept of a quantum bath that can be used to analyze the effects of measurements on the system's dynamics. Our research reveals that the Zeno and anti-Zeno effects can be observed in the strong coupling regime, as long as the measurement time is much longer than the relaxation time of the bath. This finding has the potential to be experimentally verified and serves to further our understanding of these phenomena in the context of strong coupling.

We investigate the magnetic properties of a complex spin system with certain interactions and an uneven magnetic influence. By combining two unique methods, we develop a set of basic equations that describe how the interactions and the magnetic influence impact each other. Using this framework, we calculate how the magnetic properties interact with each other at different temperatures. Additionally, we calculate how the magnetic moments interact with each other at different temperatures. The results of these calculations match well with recent simulations conducted on a specific type of quantum computer.

A novel, virtual distributed trajectory planning strategy has been developed for multi-quadrotor systems, guaranteeing the completion of tasks without collisions. The strategy integrates a centralized, multi-robot feasibility analysis with a decentralized controller, ensuring real-time computation within its own cycle. The approach relies on a linear safe zone, ensuring the path independence of trajectories, and a dynamic corridor adjustment mechanism to accommodate changing task requirements. The strategy has been proven mathematically to guarantee the system's safety and stability. The effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated through both simulated and real-world experiments, showcasing its ability to manage complex, time-varying obstacles. The real-world experiments utilized a multi-quadrotor system, comprising four quadrotors, to successfully navigate an indoor environment with changing obstacles.

Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) is a machine learning strategy that enhances the portability of models across different environments. In the context of self-driving vehicles, UDA is crucial for adapting simulation-trained models to real-world settings. Introducing CARLANE, a new benchmark that facilitates UDA training and testing, covering various real-world domains. CARLANE provides 10K labeled samples from a single simulated environment and 20K unlabeled samples across 11 diverse real-world domains. By using a semi-supervised learning approach, the labeled data is effectively utilized, making the most of the available resources. CARLANE supports multiple tasks, including lane detection and classification, as well as user-defined custom tasks. A strong baseline model is proposed, leveraging state-of-the-art UDA methods and semi-supervised learning techniques. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, achieving competitive performance with a limited 0.6% of the total dataset labeled.

Our study examines the influence of contact line dynamics on hydrogels. 
In contrast to solid substrates, hydrogels possess inherent flexibility and a high water content.
This unique combination results in a contact line that is subject to both elastic forces and capillary attraction.
To study this phenomenon, we incorporated hydrogel particles into a transparent medium and observed their behavior under gravity.
By doing so, we were able to analyze and compare the contact line behavior of hydrogels and solid objects.
Our findings indicate that hydrogels exhibit lower contact line receding angles compared to solid objects.
This data provides valuable insights into designing hydrogels for various applications, including surface wetting, cell migration, tissue engineering, and others.

A study on online learning found that connecting learners to one another can foster collaborative efforts, thus enhancing learning outcomes. A 2020 research paper explored the relationship between learners interacting with one another in a massive online course and their subsequent academic performance. The study found a positive correlation between learners' interactions and their academic results, both initially and six months later. To identify patterns in this relationship, the study grouped learners by their connectivity level and observed that those with higher connectivity tended to excel in class. Furthermore, the study revealed that a minimal threshold of learners interacting with five others is associated with the best academic results. The study also discovered that a higher proportion of diverse interactions among learners contributes to a more positive correlation between connectivity and academic results. Ultimately, the study suggests that instructors can encourage varied interactions among learners by incorporating activities that promote purposeful communication among learners who share common goals.

A new, rapid wind profiling technique has been developed utilizing 1.26 GHz Doppler radar data, primarily designed for the L-band radar wind profiler developed by a Japanese company for atmospheric observation. The technique's foundation is the autoregressive model, enabling it to accurately calculate wind speeds and directions from the uncalibrated Doppler spectra obtained directly from the field measurements. Evaluating the performance, the technique achieved an average absolute error of 0.65 m/s in wind speed and a 1.96 degrees standard deviation in wind direction, with an evaluation also conducted using a commercial X-band radar. Furthermore, the results obtained through this technique have a processing speed of around 3 seconds per range bin, allowing it to be applied for real-time data analysis.

UBC 274 is an open cluster located in the fourth quadrant of the sky, with a relatively small angular size of about 3.5 minutes and a high density of stars. This cluster contains 15 stars, 12 of which are likely members based on their spectral analysis. UBC 274 exhibits characteristics of a disrupted cluster, with its central region showing signs of expansion and its outer regions showing signs of contraction. This disruption is thought to be the result of interactions with nearby molecular clouds. Analysis of the cluster's kinematics revealed that it has a low space motion and is likely a relatively old cluster. Furthermore, it was found that the cluster's velocity dispersion is not consistent with the expectations of simple dynamical evolution, suggesting that external perturbations have played a significant role in shaping its structure. This is the first time a detailed chemical analysis of the cluster has been performed, with results showing that the abundance of elements like iron, silicon, and nickel is consistent with that of the sun. However, it was also found that the abundance of elements like sodium, aluminum, and argon is significantly higher than expected. This is likely the result of the cluster's interaction with molecular clouds.

Our research assesses whether artificial translations in a multi-lingual corpus enhance the quality of the existing bitext. We utilize a metric called the correlation distance, developed by Knoebl et al. (2020), to identify and remove artificial translations from a corpus of five languages, specifically German, English, Italian, Portuguese, and Spanish. We then re-introduce these artificial translations into the corpus and measure how they affect key metrics such as translation quality, evaluation scores, and statistical significance, particularly in the context of unsupervised MT models. Our findings indicate that incorporating artificial translations into the corpus results in consistent, yet remarkably stable, evaluation scores, particularly when using unsupervised MT models.

We have explored the phenomenon of sudden death in entanglement following the application of a specific, controlled dissipation to a spin-1/2 chain with an antiferromagnetic interaction. This process involves the creation of local spin flips at random times, triggered by the measurement of nearby spins' interactions. Initially, the entanglement's decay rate accelerates logarithmically, but its growth becomes more pronounced over time. However, due to the presence of a non-Markovian memory effect, the entanglement's rate of decay remains non-exponential. Nevertheless, in a certain long-time regime, the entanglement's growth rate becomes bounded, resulting in a shift from logarithmic decay to a saturation value. This shift is influenced by the length scale set by the cut-off frequency in the bath, and it can be viewed as a competition between entanglement generation and destruction. This study demonstrates that the entanglement's behavior can be controlled through the manipulation of the bath's properties, paving the way for the development of novel protocols in quantum technologies.

The interaction between spin and orbit within the bands of a transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) heterobilayer is examined. The findings indicate that the resulting band structure exhibits a strong spin-orbit effect, which is influenced by the orientation of spin and the symmetry of valley. The spin-orbit interaction is shown to be dependent on the crystal orientation of the TMD heterobilayer, resulting in distinct band structures that can be controlled by adjusting the orientation. The spin-orbit splitting in the flat bands of a TMD heterobilayer is found to be significantly larger than that in single-layer TMDs and is comparable to the splitting in the flat bands of graphene. The spin-orbit interaction in the flat bands of a TMD heterobilayer is shown to be large enough to enable the realization of the Mott topological phase.

In the field of quantum computing, a novel concept known as quantum reservoir computing has emerged as a supplementary tool. It involves utilizing quantum systems as computing platforms, which can be realized using various systems such as superconducting circuits and ion traps. Quantum reservoir computing allows for the processing of complex data in a manner that is beyond the capabilities of classical computing. At a fundamental level, quantum reservoir computing operates by generating a quantum state in a reservoir, which is then used to compute the input data without undergoing further processing. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of a quantum reservoir computing system, which is based on a limited-dimensional system consisting of a two-dimensional system and a one-dimensional reservoir. It demonstrates that the quantum reservoir computing system can achieve high computing accuracy, even when dealing with complex inputs. Furthermore, it shows that the computing accuracy can be improved by increasing the size of the system, which is a characteristic that is also present in classical computing. Additionally, this paper examines the computational properties of the quantum reservoir computing system, which include the computation of complex functions and the solution of eigenvalue problems. It demonstrates that the quantum reservoir computing system can effectively compute these problems, even when dealing with complex inputs.

In recent years, the pursuit of achieving quantum supremacy has led to the development of several experimental platforms, with one promising platform being the GaN/sapphire material. However, a key challenge with this material is its limited surface stability, which hinders the development of reliable devices. To overcome this issue, our study focuses on identifying the root causes of surface degradation and proposes innovative solutions to restore the integrity of the GaN surface. By implementing these solutions, we successfully restore the surface's reliability, as evident from the consistent results obtained from multiple experiments conducted at different times. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate the potential for these experiments to be scaled up to larger GaN/sapphire chips, paving the way for the successful implementation of complex quantum experiments.
