We investigate numerical approximations for approximate optimal transport problems with extensive costs, where cost functions increase with distance. These approximations must adhere to two essential criteria: they should approximate the actual solution of the problem up to a desired level of accuracy, and the resulting discrete problem should not become increasingly complex with the precision requirement. To achieve this, we develop a method combining a finite difference discretization with a reduced basis approximation of the Lagrangian, backed by theoretical convergence bounds for the solution and the Hessian. To further accelerate the computation, we reformulate the problem in an Eulerian framework and implement a limited domain decomposition to divide the computation into smaller tasks. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct numerical experiments in various dimensions.

Ramanujan found that the theta series f(z) of the form F(z+1) for a function F related to a Ramanujan-Petersson scalar invariant of level 1 satisfies modular transformation as either a power series or in a specific interval around the cusps of a congruence modular group. We show that the initial terms of such series, given by certain Hecke collections with level 1 and specific parameters, also satisfy the same transformation. We also establish similar results for generalized theta functions.

We have conducted a comprehensive analysis of the Keck ESI spectrograph's high-resolution data for eight gravitationally lensed quasars, each accompanied by a redshifted lensing galaxy. By employing a sophisticated method that models the lensing galaxy's effect on the quasar's spectrum, we have successfully isolated the quasar's emission lines from the complex lensing configurations. This approach has allowed us to determine the redshifts and velocity dispersions of both the lensing galaxies and their hosts, as well as the masses of four massive elliptical galaxies. By leveraging these findings, we have estimated the masses of the lensing galaxies within the context of the local Universe's mass function, and we have also calculated the quasars' time delays. Furthermore, we have made use of the quasars' time delays and lensing configurations to investigate the effects of time variability and lensing configurations on their observed microlensing caustic crossing events.

This paper presents a unique fixed-point theory that can be used to solve specific types of fractional differential equations. Our approach builds upon similar principles as those found in established fixed-point theories, but with the added constraint of solution uniqueness. This uniqueness is ensured by meeting specific criteria, which are defined in relation to the solution's boundary conditions and the equation itself. By employing this theory, we are able to demonstrate its efficacy in resolving a variety of nonlinear fractional differential problems.

The phonon Hall effect, discovered recently in n-type bismuth, has sparked significant interest among scientists. To better understand this phenomenon, we employed topological analysis and wound up exploring the boundaries of a phonon band structure. Utilizing a specific mathematical method known as the Wannier center calculation, we mapped out the Wannier centers of the phonon bands in a 2D representation, revealing distinct patterns that correspond to the topological features of the 2D phonon Hall effect. Notably, we observed a direct correlation between these patterns and the electric field-induced phonon Hall effect, suggesting that the topological transition plays a crucial role in the physical mechanism underlying the phonon Hall effect.

Raman spectroscopy's ability to identify molecular structures has made it a vital tool in biomedical and art research. To enhance this capability, researchers have developed broad field Raman spectroscopy, an innovative technique that allows for the analysis of multiple excitation wavelengths in a single measurement, expanding the information gathered. Building upon this technology, a new approach called shifted excitation Raman difference spectroscopy (SESERS) has been developed to significantly improve signal-to-noise ratios and reduce sample preparation time. To make SESERS a practical tool for many researchers, a novel method was developed, enabling the simultaneous collection of Raman spectra from multiple samples at different excitation wavelengths through a single measurement. This innovation, a modified version of the nod and shuffle method, has the potential to significantly expand the scope of Raman imaging and has been successfully demonstrated in a Raman microscope.
This paper introduces novel inequalities for generalized Fejér and Levin-Ste\v{c}kin matrices with entries in a Banach space.

We investigate the mean null energy condition on the event horizon of an anti-de Sitter black hole that is evaporating due to quantum effects. Our findings suggest that a certain quantum back reaction threshold must be met, implying the back reaction's influence on the black hole's null energy cannot be entirely disregarded. This conclusion is in line with a recent study on black holes in de Sitter space, where we replicated its results to validate consistency. Our research has significant implications for the information paradox theory.

This lecture notes package covers the fundamentals of $d$-dimensional Conformal Field Theory (CFT) and the associated operator product expansion, along with two specific applications. Initially, the two-point function of the stress-energy tensor is analyzed, followed by an in-depth discussion of the structure constants of operators in the theory. Furthermore, a detailed derivation of the four-point function is provided, along with an examination of the structure constants. This lecture notes package serves as a comprehensive review of 2D and 3D CFTs, along with their key characteristics.

The increasing reliance on industrial control systems has led to a significant shift towards digitalization, yet this transition overlooks the inherent flaws within existing systems. As a result, researchers have been working to develop a framework for evaluating and mitigating the various security risks associated with these systems. This research model, ICS-CTM2, is an enhanced version of the core ingredient model, CTM, designed to prioritize the security of industrial control systems. The framework identifies and weighs the importance of security measures across five distinct components: hardware, software, communication, administrative, and physical security. The security model is then applied to a specific industrial control system, the Distributed Quick Response System, in order to demonstrate its application. This research model, ICS-CTM2, is a valuable resource for researchers and professionals seeking to develop more secure digitalized industrial control systems.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning presents a significant problem, where coordinating agents to achieve a common goal is challenging due to the complexity of tracking individual and collective states. A novel approach called Avaricious-based Value Representation (AVR) has been proposed to address this issue. This method enables agents to achieve optimal coordination in cooperative learning environments by incorporating individual and collective value estimation. By leveraging the concept of avarice, agents can efficiently process sensory information and adapt to changing environments. Experimental results on various multi-agent reinforcement learning tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the AVR method, outperforming existing approaches in coordination and adapting to complex scenarios.

Our analysis examines how English-language models, pre-trained without bias information, handle stereotypical prejudice. To assess this, we've developed StereoSet: a new dataset containing 20,000 statements about prominent ethnic and racial groups in the US, along with their associated stereotypes. We've used StereoSet to test six prominent pre-trained language models (Bert-base, RoBERTa-base, GPT2-medium, XLNet-base, DistilBERT, and Deberta-v2-small) to determine if they reflect or perpetuate biased views. The results reveal that all of these models (except DistilBERT) often reference and rely on stereotypical descriptions when given a choice.

To address the issue of insufficient on-road data for developing advanced Electrical Tilt controllers using traditional methods, a novel off-policy reinforcement learning approach is applied. This method utilizes simulation data to train a controller that can transfer effectively to real-world scenarios, offering an efficient solution to optimize Electrical Tilt control policy parameters. A novel off-policy policy gradient algorithm is developed to tackle the challenges of continuous action spaces and non-linear functions. This approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the widely used Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient algorithm, showcasing robust convergence and stability. A novel off-policy evaluation method is also proposed to estimate the maximum value of a fixed Electrical Tilt policy. This method is capable of handling large-scale offline data and offers a robust estimate with theoretical guarantees. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, extensive experiments are conducted on both synthetic and real-world Electrical Tilt datasets. These experiments demonstrate the framework's ability to deliver higher system stability, better convergence, and improved controller robustness compared to existing methods.

A combination of four LHCb studies, which previously independently determined the CKM angle $\gamma$, has been performed to obtain a unified result. These studies utilized $pp$ collision data corresponding to 1.0 fb$^{-1}$ integrated luminosity, and it has been shown that this combined analysis is statistically more powerful than the individual ones, offering improved precision on $\gamma$. A standard fit that considers the $B^0 \to \pi^+\pi^-$, $B^0 \to K^+\pi^-$, and $B^{\pm} \to (B^{\mp} \to K^{0}\pi^{\pm})K^{\pm}$ angular distributions within the $B$ meson rest frame is also presented. A result of $(86.8^{+3.1}_{-2.6})^\circ$ has been obtained for $\gamma$, and it has been concluded that this combined analysis yields a more precise result than the individual ones, specifically a precision improvement on $\gamma$ of approximately 15%.

This note delves into the geometric aspects of complex ellipsoids with a quadratic structure, specifically examining their second fundamental form, as well as the real forms associated with them. Additionally, it explores several examples of complex ellipsoids to further illustrate their geometric and algebraic characteristics.

This paper investigates how non-tech savvy individuals perceive a personal data market and reacts to its presence, as part of the Plumiya initiative. In a study involving 32 participants, we explored their attitudes and behaviors, and then compared them to those of tech-savvy users involved in a previous study. Our findings suggest that even individuals lacking technical knowledge view a data exchange system much like any other digital platform, indicating that onboarding non-tech savvy users into data markets could be similar to other digital services recruitment. Moreover, our research discovered that people are inclined to sell data openly, yet express strong anxiety about giving away personal details, suggesting a delicate balance between privacy concerns and the potential for substantial financial gains that individuals weigh carefully.

In a faster-than-Nyquist (FTN) signaling environment, novel FTN receivers are proposed that leverage deep learning techniques to tackle list sphere decoding's (LSD) computational complexity. Initially, a comprehensive database of received signals is generated by simulating various FTN signaling parameters and transmitting them through an additive white Gaussian noise channel (AWGN). Subsequently, this database is labeled as "FTN symbols" and "noise" respectively. Next, a deep neural network (DNN) is trained to classify the symbols based on their respective labels. Following this, a second deep neural network (DNN) is trained to estimate the phase of transmitted symbols from the received signal. Both DNNs are then incorporated into the LSD framework, enabling it to efficiently identify the phases of transmitted symbols. As a result, a significant reduction in computational complexity of LSD is achieved for the evaluation of received signals from FTN-signaled channels. Furthermore, simulations demonstrate that the proposed DNN-based LSD outperforms the conventional LSD in terms of computational complexity, while also yielding comparable bit-error rates (BERs).

Impact algebras, a variation of fuzzy logic, are a type of transitive, commutative impact algebras with added properties of an ordered set and a specific group structure. This work involves defining the order topology and Frink ideal topology in these algebras, and it demonstrates that the order topology is equivalent to the impact algebra's interior topology when it satisfies the continuity axiom. Furthermore, it establishes a homeomorphism between certain spaces based on the Frink ideal topology, and it classifies algebras meeting the lower continuity axiom in terms of the compact-open topology.

A novel data augmentation technique, SaliencyMix, is presented to enhance image classification performance by incorporating saliency information. SaliencyMix enhances the training data by introducing random transformations to the background, guided by saliency masks, to create a more diverse dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that SaliencyMix outperforms conventional data augmentation methods, with notable improvements in models trained on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR100. Analysis indicates that the technique improves model robustness and provides valuable insights for understanding the effects of saliency masks and background modifications on feature representations.

We provide alternative proofs of the cancellation law for the infinite-dimensional Iwahori--Hecke algebra in relation to C*-algebras. Leveraging this, our research reveals that every linear map acting on $L^\infty(\mathbb{Z}_{p^\infty})$ combined with an affine linear map on $\mathbb{Z}_{p^\infty}$ constitutes a proper trace within the Iwahori--Hecke algebra. Furthermore, our study identifies a specific set of "generalized traces," which encompasses all other traces defined on the Iwahori--Hecke algebra.

A new method is proposed for detecting gravitational theories by combining data on galaxy orientation with that of cosmic distortion. This method is particularly suitable for detecting and testing gravitational theories at smaller scales than previously possible. A simulation of the intrinsic alignment of galaxies in the LSST survey is conducted, and its correlation with cosmic shear is considered. This allows for a comparison of the relative importance of cosmic distortion and intrinsic alignment due to galaxy orientation. This technique enables the detection of altered gravity models, such as those predicted by Horndeski gravity, by using the first two moments of the intrinsic alignment matrix. This method is found to be more effective than other methods, such as those that measure higher-order statistics, due to the larger sample size and wider survey area. This technique is also found to be more resilient to systematic errors that occur during data collection.

In a simulation, we explored the movement of a group of flexible beads under the influence of pressure, aligning with a laboratory study on similar material. We discovered that applying a constant pressure results in an unusual type of flow with negative viscosity and a tendency to form a permanent pattern of patterns with 6-fold symmetry. We attribute these properties to the balance between stretching and relaxation of the flexible nature of the material. Furthermore, we observed that increasing the flexibility of the material leads to a transition from a state where patterns change rapidly to a state where patterns change slowly.

The use of photo-induced gold nanoparticle melting as a trigger mechanism in complex systems has garnered attention in recent years due to its adaptability. However, the existing models which describe this process rely heavily on empirical data and can be difficult to apply in new situations. In an effort to address this limitation, a novel approach is proposed which integrates a physics-based model with machine learning. This approach utilizes a semi-classical model that simulates the melting of gold nanoparticles and a neural network that models the semi-classical model's inputs. The trained neural network can then be used to estimate the melting temperature of gold nanoparticles of varying sizes and shapes, regardless of their specific structure. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated using a dataset of nanoparticles with different shapes and sizes, and it is shown that the trained neural network accurately reproduces the results from the semi-classical model.

We establish a parameterized version of the Fredholm operator theory, tailored for bounded linear operators acting on Banach spaces. The resulting theory enables the precise analysis of parameterized families of linear operators, and in turn, facilitates the investigation of various nonlinear phenomena. In the context of bounded linear operators acting between Banach spaces $X$ and $Y$, our approach yields a parameterized version of the principle of linearisatio, where it is shown that solutions to infinite-dimensional parameterized complement problems consistently vary in a'smooth' manner. Furthermore, this work provides the necessary mathematical tools to examine the smoothness properties of solutions in various infinite-dimensional complement problems, including complement problems for $C^2$ functions, differential equations, variational inequalities, variational problems and degree theory problems. In the following part of the paper, this framework is applied to differential operators.

Within the framework of the flavor theory of mind, the brain's taste processing centers are strongly linked to an individual's cognitive abilities. This paper delves into the relationships between taste perception, cognitive performance, and emotional state through an innovative approach, introducing a unique taste tetrahedron. Our investigation examined how taste influences emotions and cognitive functions, revealing a notable correlation between the taste of sweetness and improved memory recall. Additionally, a sweet tooth has been found to be indicative of future depression, serving as an early indicator for individuals who may be more susceptible to mental health disorders. This research marks a significant milestone in its analysis of the interplay among taste, emotions, and cognitive functions, paving the way for a deeper understanding of human behavior.

This paper's primary objective is to derive new, distinct equations involving the (h; q)-Genocchi numbers and polynomials with various parameters. We will leverage the inverse of the (h; q)-Genocchi numbers of the second kind under the p-adic q-Bernstein polynomials on Zp to achieve this goal.

This study introduces a novel machine learning technique to determine the long-term effects of treatments on patient outcomes by analyzing electronic health records. The proposed method involves a two-stage approach: the first stage uses a deep neural network to predict short-term patient responses to treatments, and the second stage uses a probabilistic model to simulate patient trajectories over the long term. By integrating these stages, the method can provide a comprehensive estimate of long-term treatment effects. The approach was tested using a large-scale dataset from the Veterans Affairs healthcare system and demonstrated its ability to accurately estimate treatment effects. The method's performance was comparable to established statistical methods, but with the added advantage of being non-parametric and flexible. The proposed method has the potential to be widely applicable in real-world settings to support decision-making and improve patient care.

To address the effect of recall distortion in case-control studies, we developed a semi-parametric model that accounts for distinct recall functions in cases and controls. We employed a Monte Carlo algorithm to estimate the parameters, alongore analyzing its asymptotic behavior to derive an estimator for the relative risk. We validated the method through a study on type 2 diabetes and hyperuricemia link, utilizing data from the Asturias Study. The outcome showed that the estimated RR value was 1.5 (95% CI: 1.25-2.16), indicating a possible causal relationship. We further explored the method's efficiency by comparing it to a case-control study without adjustment and discovered that the adjusted relative risk estimates were doubled.

Generative autoencoders are a type of model that can be trained in two stages: first, as a traditional bottleneck-based autoencoder, or alternatively, as a generative model that's trained to produce the same data distribution it was trained on. However, the standard training method for these models has a significant drawback when it comes to estimating maximum likelihood, as it often results in inaccurate variance estimates. This issue is particularly pronounced in scenarios where the data distribution is highly concentrated. To overcome this limitation, a new, more efficient and reliable method for training generative autoencoders has been developed. This new approach leverages the properties of specific types of neural networks that can easily reverse direction, which allows for a more straightforward and efficient estimation of maximum likelihood. The proposed method can be used to train a wide range of models, including those with multiple layers, and can be easily integrated into existing training algorithms. The results of simulations and real-world testing demonstrate the effectiveness of this new approach.

In today's fast-paced urban environments, decision-makers face a multitude of complex urban issues, making it difficult to pinpoint key factors and their interactions. To address this challenge, we've developed an interactive visualization tool that empowers users to analyze relationships between multiple features within urban data sets. Our approach allows users to select the data points of interest and gain insight into the most critical characteristics associated with them, thereby identifying patterns and connections from the data itself. Furthermore, our system offers a pattern search function that enables users to investigate similarities and differences in feature patterns and streamline their analysis work, ultimately simplifying their research goals and objectives.

This study introduces an algebraic multigrid preconditioner suitable for HDG-P0 finite element methods applied to a broad category of linear problems. Initially, we establish a novel coercivity bound for the HDG-P0 matrix derived from the reaction-diffusion equation. Subsequently, we develop an MRCM preconditioner that leverages geometric information to enhance its performance. The preconditioner's effectiveness is demonstrated through various numerical experiments showcasing its efficiency and reliability.

Missing data can lead to biased and unsound results. To address this issue, we suggest a novel Bayesian method for evaluating how different variables affect missing data in survey responses. This approach involves calculating the E-value, a probability-like measure that compares the odds of observed data in the relevant region. Within a Bayesian framework, we initially assess the likelihood of data being missing and then derive a posterior distribution for the E-value. Our method allows for the calculation of credible intervals for the E-value, which can be used to determine whether observed data patterns are statistically significant. This methodology is demonstrated through a practical application in the Consumer Expenditure Survey.

A recent study by Hsu et al. (2019) introduced a probability-based approach to assess the missing information in a crossover trial with multiple endpoints. This paper extends this concept by developing a more efficient estimator for evaluating missing information in a complex crossover design involving multiple endpoints. We derive a closed-form solution for calculating the missing information in a particular sequence of two-group crossover trials with multiple endpoints. Our approach also allows us to compare the missing information in a single-group trial with multiple endpoints to that in a single endpoint trial with varying sample sizes. Furthermore, we examine the properties of our estimator, including its asymptotic behavior and bias. Simulation studies confirm that our estimator produces unbiased and symmetrical estimates of missing information. An example case is provided to demonstrate the practical application of our methodology.

This passage outlines the basics of the Stasheff A(n)-theory and explores its relevance to categorical studies in the context of category theory. It also touches on related concepts such as Kan's structure and the problems associated with Loday's deformation theory. Furthermore, the discussion covers the notion of a monoidal equivalent and provides a brief introduction to a modern approach to generalizing the Stasheff A(n)-theory. The primary challenge of this approach is to generalize the theory to categories with non-positive homotopy types. A key challenge in this endeavor is the study of feeble monoidal categories, of which a notable example is the category of simple Lie algebras.

The growing demand for main memory upgrades is driving the search for innovative solutions to enhance existing DRAM technology. The introduction of in-drain memory (IDM) has the potential to boost the performance and efficiency of DRAM. The development of IDM, however, is hindered by the significant costs associated with it. To make IDM more accessible to memory manufacturers and hardware designers, a cost-effective substrate is needed. This work presents codic, a cost-efficient substrate that enables the integration of IDM features and optimizations, specifically bimodal voltage (BMV) and resistance trending (RTM), into standard DRAM technology. The proposed system, codic, incorporates BMV and RTM into DRAM without increasing chip area, manufacturing costs, or power consumption. Performance evaluations demonstrate that codic, coupled with BMV and RTM, outperforms DRAM by 11% and 28% in terms of geometric mean for memory-intensive workloads.

The integration of VNS with 5G networks is a natural progression, building on existing infrastructure and software to create sophisticated virtualized networks. This paper delves into the concept of virtualized network assets within the context of 5G, focusing on how functional programming can facilitate their administration and orchestration. By examining the challenges posed by network evolution and addressing them with a design approach, the paper aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of virtualized networks. Through the use of functional programming, the paper demonstrates how such networks can be designed, modeled, and optimized for efficient operation.

To explore the relationship between the performance of quantum error correction and the quality of the noise affecting the system, we investigate a toric code system. In this context, we're interested in how the type of noise - whether it's localized or not - influences the characteristics of the code. To address this, we introduce a noise model that allows for the manipulation of noise correlations and demonstrate how it's possible to control the noise distribution by varying the geometry of the toric code. Through simulations, we examine the effects of noise on both single and multiple qubits and observe distinct correlations resulting from the manipulation of noise correlations. In these simulations, we identify the optimal conditions for creating a noise-free environment and analyze the error rates of the multi-qubit operations within this noise-free space.

The OPUS system is a universal job management system that fully adheres to VO
standards. It not only supports standard protocols, such as GridJob and GWES, but
also furnishes a management system capable of managing jobs of any complexity in
a secure, sandboxed environment. OPUS is a comprehensive tool that enables the
management of multiple jobs, including those submitted via web interface, and
supports advanced features like job submission and proxy management via GWES UI.
This document details the development and functionality of OPUS, including its
technical requirements and future plans.

The field of wireless networks is rapidly expanding, with an abundance of research and literature available. However, traditional educational approaches often fail to engage students due to their complexity and traditional nature, focusing primarily on theoretical knowledge rather than practical applications. Moreover, current educational methods lack interactivity, making it difficult for students to understand the dynamics of wireless networks and how they can impact real-world systems. In response, we developed an educational platform called the "Wireless Network Game," which combines game-enhanced learning to provide an immersive and engaging experience for students. Our initial findings reveal that the game is an effective tool for instruction, with our study indicating that it not only increases students' understanding of wireless networks but also enhances their willingness to learn and participate in future educational activities.

The widely accepted ozone-proximity indicator for the habitability range of a planet has been tested against a comprehensive model of the Earth's atmosphere, revealing inconsistencies that challenge its validity as a proxy across diverse atmospheric conditions. The model, which considers various atmospheric and stellar variables, shows that other indicators, such as the biosignature of O2, carbon dioxide and methane, may offer more reliable proxy values for planetary habitability. The model also suggests that O2's lifetime may be influenced by its mixing with CO2, further undermining the proxy's accuracy. The study's findings have significant implications for the development of habitability indicators and the search for life beyond our planet.

In the quantum Hofstadter model, we've created stable, non-equilibrium current flows along the edge of a two-dimensional lattice when subjected to a combination of magnetic fields, moat fields, and periodic driving of the lattice. These driven currents are resistant to changes in the magnetic field or moat field, as long as their ratios remain constant. The origin of these currents lies in the quantized cyclotron motion of the electrons, which is preserved by the moat fields. The lattice then injects a forward-moving edge current that remains robust. The unique topological characteristics of the Hofstadter model allow these currents to withstand modifications to the lattice structure, such as the introduction of a gap or the application of a magnetic field gradient. The potential applications of these currents in quantum metrology and information processing are vast.

Recent advancements in Multilingual Neural Machine Translation (MNMT) have led to significant performance improvements. However, these models often struggle when exposed to domains outside their trained scope. In this study, we examine the impact of domain-specific fine-tuning on MNMT models in a medical context. We evaluate two models with training on the MedNLI dataset and fine-tuning on either clinical notes or medical abstracts. Our findings suggest that domain-specific adjustments can improve performance in specific scenarios, although no universal benefits were observed.

A theoretical analysis of the influence of positively charged particles on the characteristics of modified-ion-acoustic waves has been conducted. The study, which considered a two-component plasma system consisting of hot electrons, warm positive ions, nonthermal electrons, and positive charged particles, utilized a fluid approach to model the species and an ambipolar potential to describe it. The investigation revealed that the presence of positively charged particles can lead to the formation of both solitary and shock waves, and that their concentration and charge-to-mass ratio significantly impact the waves' speed and amplitude. Furthermore, the study demonstrated that the presence of warm positive ions and high-energy electrons can lead to the formation of both types of waves, and that their density and energy levels affect the waves' characteristics. The findings suggest that positively charged particles can be used to control the formation of both solitary and shock waves, and that they can be applied in various space and astrophysical plasma environments.

Recent advancements in multilingual information retrieval have seen significant improvements through pretraining techniques that leverage dense sentence embeddings and mask language modeling. However, applying these methods to unsupervised settings has proven challenging, particularly when adapting between languages. To address this, our research proposes a novel approach to unsupervised sentence embedding for multilingual information retrieval, focusing on contextual understanding. By incorporating a language identifier and sentence separator, our method successfully trains and applies sentence embeddings across diverse languages, enhancing performance in a variety of applications, including sentence similarity, relevance, and dense retrieval ranking.

In the field of multimodal education, we focus on enhancing the learning experience for students by leveraging the strengths of multiple learning approaches.
A significant challenge in this area is the imbalance of learning modes, which hinders the effective integration of multiple modalities. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework called PMR that uses a unique representation of multiple modalities to identify and mitigate the limitations of individual learning approaches. Specifically, PMR exploits the distinct characteristics of each learning mode by comparing its representations to a set of representative examples. This approach allows PMR to identify and capitalize on the unique strengths of each learning mode, leading to improved performance. We demonstrate the efficacy of PMR in a multimodal education setting, where we combine the capabilities of natural language and visual learning approaches. The results show that PMR achieves notable improvements in both accuracy and efficiency, outperforming existing methods by 8.1% in accuracy and 11.2% in accuracy per hour.

This research expands on conveyance theory, incorporating vector engagement to account for the interplay between various types of engagement, such as social and structural engagement, which can switch roles as either sources or sinks. The specific model employed in this study involves a coupled system of two reaction-diffusion equations, one governing conveyance theory and the other representing vector engagement. Analyzing this system yields two key outcomes: the derivation of wave equation-like equations for conveyance and vector engagement, and a general expression for the combined dynamics of these processes. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that when both conveyance and vector engagement are active, the system's eigenfunctions exhibit a continuous spectrum, resulting in unbounded growth of the associated eigenvalues.

This study introduces a new method for efficiently representing spoken command recognition data, leveraging low-rank data representations and machine learning techniques. Standard deep learning models are impractical due to the significant storage requirements of spoken command datasets. To mitigate this, we employ a three-dimensional data structure using tensor decomposition, allowing us to reduce storage needs and speed up data processing. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach can achieve comparable results to standard models, such as convolutional and residual networks, while also being more lightweight. Furthermore, we explore the potential of combining different data structures within a single network to enhance performance. Our findings suggest that this approach can result in better accuracy while incurring only a minor increase in computational expense compared to using standard network structures.

The concept of quantum jumps, a fundamental approach to understanding the behavior of open quantum systems, is explored in depth. By delving into the underlying algebraic structure of the Lindblad master equation, a clear distinction is drawn between quantum jumps that arise from linear and circular master equations. A deeper analysis of the circular representation reveals a unique property, where its corresponding jump operators form a group. Consequently, there exists a finite number of distinct quantum jumps that can be observed. These distinct jumps are then used to create various number sequences, such as Fibonacci and Lucas numbers, and a specific number of jumps is used to recreate a well-known (3+1)-level open quantum system dynamics.

Enhancing the absorption of solar photons in thin-film silicon solar cells is crucial for increasing their efficiency. This can be achieved through the incorporation of metallic nanoparticles that complement silicon-junction solar cells. By strategically combining metal nanoparticles with existing junctions, it is possible to boost the solar cell's absorption capabilities. This research investigates the effects of aluminum plasmonic nanoparticles within a silicon thin-film solar cell on its absorption properties. By employing the finite-difference time-domain method and a numerical model, this study examines the influence of various parameters such as diameter, height, and concentration of these aluminum nanoparticles on the silicon solar cell's absorption. The results indicate that aluminum plasmonic nanoparticles can significantly enhance the solar cell's absorption when carefully positioned near the silicon-oxygen-silicon interface. The diameter and height of these nanoparticles play crucial roles in this process, with optimal values found to be 20-25% of the silicon film's thickness. The concentration of these nanoparticles should not exceed 10% of the solar cell's thickness to avoid detrimental effects on its absorption properties.

The field of descriptive complexity in logic is being examined to determine if it can account for computational complexity classes without relying on complex enumeration constructs. This study aims to establish a link between logic and complexity classes by exploring a modular, logic-based framework to represent polynomial-time computation. In this framework, a linear-time computation is represented by a first-order logic formula with universal and existential quantifiers, specifically through the lens of a two-variable logic. By introducing a novel, existential quantifier inspired by second-order logic, the researchers found that a suitable choice of this operator can effectively capture the class PTIME of polynomial-time computable functions. This study also examines the impact of alternative enumeration operators and provides a comprehensive analysis of the proposed framework.

LSTM networks have become a leading deep learning technique for video analysis, but their high complexity hinders their implementation on low-power devices. To address this limitation, we developed an end-to-end co-design system that optimizes LSTM network architecture and hardware to achieve energy efficiency. Our system first identifies the most energy-wasting operations during training, then uses tensor decomposition to minimize unnecessary calculations. We integrated our decomposed model into hardware accelerators using Hierarchical Tucker Decomposition and a novel mapping technique. Our system was applied to an LSTM video analysis network, and we created a customized processor with 16 cores to analyze 8-second video clips. The results show that our optimized hardware accelerators achieve significant energy savings: the total energy consumption is reduced by 7.2 times when decomposing 3D tensors using our mapping technique compared to a standard approach.

The MAVLink protocol, used by popular UAV systems like Ardupilot and PX4, has been widely adopted in the UAV industry. However, its security has not received sufficient attention until now. Given the critical nature of MAVLink, we conducted a security analysis to identify potential risks and developed MAVSec, a secure solution for the protocol. Our research revealed several security vulnerabilities in the protocol, enabling various attacks such as system crashes, malicious control, and data manipulation. To address these issues, we created MAVSec, a secure server, which filters incoming commands from clients and ensures only authorized requests are processed. We also developed MAVCmd, a command-line tool for testing and executing commands, as well as MAVVis, a visualization tool for enhancing user experience. Our proposed solution has been thoroughly evaluated, and MAVSec has been successfully integrated into Ardupilot, a widely-used UAV software.

The concept of emulation refers to generating a lesser-level version of a complex system that replicates its behavior, often through a simpler model. In this research, we introduce a novel approach to create dynamic distributed systems, analogous to systems that utilize virtual nodes, by incorporating emulation techniques. We demonstrate that the emulation framework is capable of effectively simulating complex, distributed, and dynamic environments, without requiring modifications to the underlying system logic or logic implementation. Our results show that the distributed emulation structure is resistant to changes in the number of participating nodes and variable computation times, resulting in predictable and linear behavior.

The Newman-Penrose map can be naturally extended to complexified null cones, providing an alternative representation of complexified Ashtekar variables. This variable transformation can be seen as a natural extension of the complexified Lorentzian twistor lift, which in turn encompasses both the Newman-Penrose and spin coefficient formalisms. The complexified Newman-Penrose formalism can be directly derived from the complexified Lorentzian twistor lift, offering a straightforward method to describe solutions to the Einstein equations in terms of complex Ashtekar variables.

The Muon Detector, a cutting-edge tool, utilizes highly energetic muons as a tracer to map the subterranean environment with exceptional precision. The Muon Detector, a state-of-the-art system, combines advanced tracking technology with precision detectors to monitor the subterranean environment with high sensitivity. The Muon Detector's innovative design enables the detection of underground objects with remarkable accuracy, utilizing highly energetic muons as a tracer to produce detailed tomographic images of the subterranean Earth. The Muon Detector's exceptional sensitivity, facilitated by the weak interaction between matter and muons, allows it to detect objects as small as a few kilograms per square meter. The device's capabilities are further enhanced by its exceptional direction resolution, enabling the precise tracking of muon trajectories, and the incorporation of additional sensors to monitor the surrounding environment. The Muon Detector's remarkable features, including its high sensitivity, direction resolution, and ability to detect underground objects, makes it an invaluable tool for subterranean tomography.

A new parser framework has been proposed, employing a parsing expression grammar that defines production rules directly. 
Below is an example parsing expression grammar using this framework, applied to a simple arithmetic calculator language that allows for integer multiplication and addition operations combined with variables. 
The parser generation leverages a generalized pushdown automaton, which offers a more detailed exploration of parsing mechanisms than traditional pushdown automata. 
The parser's performance is enhanced through the use of parallel call stacks for its function calls and a single thread for the rest of its operations. 
The code can be run in a real-world scenario where variables with the same name from different scopes are parsed.

In this research, we investigate the properties of a classical abelian Proca theory within the framework of a four-dimensional Euclidean field theory at a non-zero temperature. Specifically, we examine the conditions necessary for the theory to exhibit a vacuum Cherenkov radiation. We also derive the effective action governing the theory's behavior in the deep infrared regime, where the magnetic field is weak, and demonstrate that it can be described by a modified Nambu-Jona-Latin model with a specific parameter. Furthermore, we identify the conditions under which the theory's effective action predicts the emergence of a vacuum Cherenkov radiation within the context of a renormalization group analysis.

To enhance our understanding of language, researchers can utilize cutting-edge neural language models that draw upon massive databases of text. These advanced models exhibit remarkable performance in predicting and understanding language, yet their underlying data and processing limitations remain unclear. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted a study where we taught two prominent neural language models – GPT-2 and T5, and compared their performance with a state-of-the-art model based on Transformer architecture (XLM-R). We then compared their results with those from a simple model based on a 2017 paper by Ammar etassistant et al. that was trained on a smaller, less diverse dataset. Our research found that the XLM-R model outperformed all others in forecasting language, including the GPT-2 and GPT-3 models. Furthermore, our study revealed that the XLM-R model's performance is not solely dependent on its size but rather heavily relies on the quality of its training data.

A novel approach to determining the three-dimensional positioning of a visual system utilizes the observation of one or more objects rotating within it. This concept, dubbed unintentional turntables, is particularly relevant in scenarios where direct measurements are not feasible. A key innovation involves employing a neural network that integrates information about an object's 3D shape along with its rotation, thereby inducing a mapping between visual appearances and 3D configurations. Notably, this network can be trained without visual examples from the target visual system. We have successfully demonstrated the effectiveness of this method in two distinct applications: reconstructing the 3D positioning of a camera after capturing a single image of a rotating object, and utilizing the appearance of a rotating car to determine the 3D positioning of a series of street-level images taken by a mobile device.

In a quantum dot connected to superconducting and normal metal leads via barriers, we examine the transport characteristics through quantum interference of Andreev bound states. When a barrier's height is modulated, while its width remains constant, the ratio of $r$, representing reflected Andreev states, and $t$, denoting transmitted conduction electrons, can be adjusted. This ratio significantly influences the current through the quantum dot, with its sign determining whether the dot operates in an inductive or superinductive state. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the crossover between these states can be triggered by tuning the barrier height, leading to a substantial current, and we also show that the co-tunneling of both conduction electrons and Cooper pairs is contingent upon the specific barrier height.

A new model has been developed to explain the rapid acceleration of particles during magnetic reconnection, drawing from an earlier theory that used an ad-hoc scattering mechanism to account for particles moving across field lines. This mechanism can be represented by a simple equation that determines the rate at which particles scatter in angle. By applying this equation to a simplified 2D model of reconnection, it was shown that the required scattering rate is relatively low, comparable to the rate at which particles move along field lines. This mechanism was found to be essential in two scenarios: when the reconnecting magnetic field is highly inclined and when it is oriented almost perpendicular to the current sheet. This model offers a more efficient and physically plausible alternative to previous theories that relied on turbulent fluctuations or chaotic electron orbits, making it potentially useful for explaining particle acceleration in a wider range of reconnection scenarios.

In this research, we examine the potential for detecting extended scalar sectors at the International Electron-Proton Collider. The machine learning-based analysis focuses on identifying a light Higgs boson decaying into a $Z$-boson and a photon in the diphoton final state, as well as its implications on the study of extended scalar sectors. The theoretical framework is based on the Minimal R-symmetric Supersymmetric Model, which includes a well-motivated Higgs sector consisting of four non-interacting scalar doublets. The model's Higgs sector can be broken down into five CP-even scalars, which can be reduced to three physical Higgs states. The analysis assumes that the mass difference between the SM-like Higgs boson and the second CP-even scalar is significant, which can be used to determine the mass of the second CP-even scalar. The study demonstrates that the International Electron-Proton Collider can be used to detect the second CP-even scalar with a significance of 5σ at 500 GeV center-of-mass energy with 4 ab^-1 luminosity. The research also examines the impact of the second CP-even scalar on the branching ratio of the SM-like Higgs boson decaying into a photon pair. The analysis reveals that the branching ratio can be suppressed by up to 2% and 4% respectively at 500 GeV center-of-mass energy with 4 ab^-1 luminosity.

This paper examines the subdifferential of the collective numerical radius, a function initially presented in "Collective Numerical Range" by Bhatia-Nagata, along with identifying some essential elements.

The widespread use of data in today's world has led to an increase in data privacy concerns. As a result, researchers have proposed a new model called FPC, which stands for Federated Pricing with Contracts, to address these issues. In this approach, two main actors, a price setter and a price taker, interact to achieve a balance. The price setter collects data from the price taker, then uses that data to set prices. Conversely, the price taker supplies goods to the price setter based on the set prices. Our research focuses on implementing a new protocol called FPC that incorporates a monetary mechanism to ensure the privacy of sensitive information. We have developed a new algorithm, MP-EP, which allows for a wide range of data types, including binary, continuous, and categorical. Our proposed model, FPC, has been tested with real-world datasets, including the well-known Adult and Iris datasets, to demonstrate its effectiveness. Our findings show that FPC not only preserves data privacy but also achieves a high level of accuracy.

We introduce a novel concept of stochastic assignment, drawing from Shapley and Stobaeck's (2009) work, which focuses on random allocation fields. This involves partitioning a sample space into subsets and assigning a probability of allocation to each, while also considering the potential for multiple assignments occurring simultaneously. This novel framework is then applied to analyze real-valued functions over a compact set with countably infinite dimensions, using the concept of stochastic assignment correlation to capture the relationship between functions. This analysis is further developed to provide an alternative representation, which reveals that stochastic assignment correlation can be viewed as a weighted form of expected inner product correlation. This provides an additional perspective on the correlation approach introduced by van der Laan and Gruber (2011).

The combustion of hydrogen-containing fuels poses a significant risk due to the potential for explosive mixtures to form. To better understand and prevent these explosions, researchers have been studying the process of initiating combustion under high pressure using lasers. A new study investigated the use of a laser to initiate combustion in a high-pressure mixture of hydrogen, oxygen, and helium, with a focus on how different energy levels and gas conditions affect the process. A significant finding was that the energy added to the gas layer plays a key role in determining the outcome, with a threshold energy required to initiate combustion, which increases with pressure. To better understand the process, researchers used a combination of theoretical and computational models to analyze the process in detail. A key challenge was the lack of a precise description of the energy absorbed by the gas layer, which researchers addressed by developing a new model that takes into account the properties of the gas. A comparison with experimental data showed that the model was able to accurately predict the process. A key outcome of the study was the development of a new map that predicts the likelihood of combustion based on energy and pressure conditions. A significant finding was that the process of combustion is more complex than previously thought, with a key transition occurring at a specific energy threshold. The study's results have important implications for understanding the process of ignition and preventing the buildup of explosive energy in high-pressure gas mixtures.

To achieve accurate segmentation, it is crucial to analyze the local characteristics of image pixels. However, existing methods such as CNN-based approaches fail to consider the inherent characteristics of object boundaries, resulting in inadequate image segmentation. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a new deep learning-based boundary-aware segmentation network (BBNet) that leverages local pixel features and their spatial relationships to enhance segmentation accuracy. The BBNet incorporates a novel boundary recognition module that combines pixel-level boundary features with a global boundary map, resulting in improved image segmentation. Comprehensive evaluations of the BBNet on multiple benchmark datasets reveal that our method outperforms other leading techniques in terms of segmentation accuracy.

Automated vehicles with advanced communication capabilities can enhance road safety by sharing vital information with one another. Current research focuses on developing a network that enables vehicles to send and receive location-specific messages, facilitating cooperation on the road. Our study centers on creating a driver-messenger network by distributing an information diffusion platform, allowing drivers to enhance road safety awareness. Specifically, this system facilitates the lane shift assistance, an essential cooperative driving maneuver that enhances traffic flow. Our experiment involved a simulation study examining the effects of the information diffusion platform's key factors on its performance, along with a real-world experiment conducted in a traffic setting to evaluate its potential benefits.

Researchers have been studying the behavior of inactive particles by simulating them as being affected by a random force and resistance to flow. These "freeely active" particles are often modeled as being influenced by diffusion driven by the random force and resistance to flow. In some environments, the rate of a particle leaving a certain area can be calculated based on the area's size and boundary properties. In this paper, the researchers investigate the behavior of these particles when they are confined to different shapes and see how the area's boundary properties affect their behavior. They discovered that for a circular environment with a certain radius, the rate at which a particle leaves the area can be calculated using a simple formula. In other shapes such as rectangles and more complex areas like Mobius surfaces, the researchers found that the rate at which a particle leaves the area can be calculated using certain properties of the area but not others.

For an atom consisting of $N$ electrons, we consider the ground state of the Hartree model with its $N$ particles confined to a 2D area. In this setting, the confinement potential is a soft wall defined as $\omega(\mathbf{x})=\omega_0+\omega_1|\mathbf{x}|^2$, with a gap existing between the ground state energy levels and the infinite particle number limit. Specifically, this gap is within the range of $O(\omega_0+N^{-1})$ and $O(|\ln N|^{-1})$.

Observations of the Si IV 1390\,nm line in a solar flare captured by the IRIS satellite reveal rapid changes in both the line's intensity and shape, occurring in a matter of seconds. These fluctuations, which cannot be attributed to changes in nonthermal energy or viewing angle, suggest a highly dynamic environment, with ions being heated to millions of degrees in just seconds. Changes in line profiles were found to be non-isotropic and show evidence of both thermal and non-thermal motions occurring simultaneously, potentially indicating the presence of both shock-heated and coronal plasmas. Further analysis suggests that the coronal plasma is being heated to temperatures exceeding 1 million Kelvin in a matter of milliseconds.

The Peccei-Quinn mechanism's original form is shown to be insufficient in explaining all aspects of axion physics. A more general, time-varying CP symmetry is proposed which can be broken at a scale significantly higher than the QCD scale. At low energies, this results in an effective theory that includes a massless vector-like axion particle and an electric dipole moment, which is a natural consequence of this scenario. The implications of this scenario on the search for axion dark matter and the electric dipole moment of nucleons are explored.

The impact of collision cascades on optical properties in irradiated materials is a crucial consideration for various nanofabrication techniques. To investigate this, we simulated a non-uniform $^{4}He$ ion distribution within a $0.1\,\mu\rm m$ thick silicon layer. The resulting Raman scattering and refractive index modifications were calculated, and the simulations revealed that the presence of localized He ion clusters can alter the critical angle for total reflection. This effect is attributed to enhanced non-radiative decay of the $\gamma$-transition in the $1s_{1/2}^{9}+1s_{1/2}^*$ state, which is facilitated by the high ionization potential of silicon. The simulations also showed that the density of He ions and the ion fluence have a significant influence on the process, as do the energy of the ions and the fluctuations in ion distribution.

Protecting software from unauthorized reproduction is a difficult task. To safeguard against unauthorized copying or the open-source distribution of commercial software, an innovative approach called source code anti-copying has been developed. The Navigation Approach, a novel watermarked-based method, aims to detect and prevent such unauthorized distribution by adding navigable watermarks to the software. This method utilizes a secret key to prevent unauthorized removal or alteration of watermarks, making it a robust solution. A case study using C# code demonstrates the effectiveness of the Navigation Approach, which was implemented using.NET and Windows Forms to embed navigable watermarks as system-generated metadata. The verification process, performed on a separate computer, utilized a client-server framework and a secret key to confirm the software's authenticity and combat watermark removal techniques.

The article explores the full convergence of certain automorphic Dirichlet series. Initially, the criteria for full convergence on complex planes are established; next, the relationship between full convergence and the strong Poisson-Vinogradov criterion is examined; and finally, the complete convergence of automorphic series along exponential directions is considered. Key findings include: the complete convergence of automorphic Dirichlet series along non-polynomial exponential directions in the case of thin groups; the full convergence of automorphic Dirichlet series on complex planes when the strong Poisson-Vinogradov criterion is met; and under the assumption of Diophantine properties for these groups, the complete convergence of automorphic Dirichlet series along polynomial exponential directions is demonstrated, provided the exponent is less than the dimension of the group.

This letter demonstrates that every complete metric space X with the property that the metric charaterizes all mappings from subsets of X to X that are bounded in distance, is itself a subset of a larger complete metric space Y. This result implies a new proof of the fixed point theorem for bounded distance mappings in the metric space. Additionally, we show that the property extends to non-complete metric spaces with finite topological dimension, addressing an earlier question posed by J. Smillie.

We propose a new type of distribution, referred to as M\"obius log-concave (MLC), which is parameterized by $n+2$ values. Notably, MLC distributions can be generated in polynomial time and exhibit desirable properties including log-conconcavity and a finite support of size $n$. Building on this, we develop efficient algorithms to estimate log-concave probability density functions in one dimension using data samples, which are capable of producing estimates with a total variation distance of $O(1/\sqrt{n})$ with high probability when $n$ is large. Our approach relies on a novel class of MLC distributions and a new type of spline called a log-concave M\"obius spline, which is capable of being computed in polynomial time.

We have developed a novel approach to efficiently identify and count microstates of granular systems with fixed positions, which is essential for understanding their non-equilibrium behavior. This method, which is based on the Wang-Landau algorithm, allows us to map and explore the entire microstate space of the system, and it has been successfully applied to a 2D granular system with varying density and boundary conditions. Our results show that the algorithm is highly efficient and can be used to identify and count microstates with high accuracy, and it is particularly useful in systems with complex microstates, which are difficult to analyze using traditional methods. Overall, this approach provides a powerful tool for analyzing and understanding the microstate spaces of a wide range of non-equilibrium granular systems.

We introduce a new graph theory problem known as the Adventurer-Manager game, a strategic game that pits two players against each other, Adventurer and Manager. Their goal is complex: Adventurer aims to visit every vertex of a designated graph, while Manager must prevent this by selectively deleting vertices. However, Adventurer is granted the opportunity to substitute an unvisited vertex of the same degree as the deleted one. Despite this advantage, Adventurer can guarantee a win regardless of Manager's initial moves. Conversely, if the graph has a vertex with infinite degree, Adventurer can only force Manager to lose. Interestingly, if the graph is planar, Manager can also ensure victory. Furthermore, we explore Adventurer's winning conditions for various types of graphs, such as trees, cycles, and complete graphs, as well as present open questions regarding the remaining cases.

This paper explores how frequencies in Gaussian processes relate to each other over time. It begins with a mathematical model describing the probability of a particle moving at various speeds, accounting for random changes in direction. By solving complex differential equations, the study finds the probability of a particle having a specific speed at a specific time. It then calculates a spectral density that corresponds to this probability, and shows how this density changes over both the particle's speed and time. Furthermore, the research reveals that different pairs of these densities are linked through specific correlations and demonstrates how these correlations work using an example based on an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process.

This paper examines one-dimensional higher-order Broer-Kaup systems, which represent two-dimensional systems of partial differential equations of the form $\partial_t^m u_1 + \partial_t^j \partial_x^m J_1u_1=0$ and $\partial_t^m \overline{u}_1+\partial_t^m \partial_x^m \overline{J}_1\overline{u}_1=0$. The study focuses on the higher-order Broer-Kaup system, which is a reduction of the two-dimensional Dym equation, a system that is completely integrable and integrable. The solutions of this system are generated by multi-soliton solutions and are the foundation for understanding higher-order Dym systems. The solutions of this system are also applied to the study of various physical models, such as the dynamics of the ocean and the behavior of shallow water waves. The main goal of this paper is to develop a method for the exact solution of the higher-order Broer-Kaup system, which is a challenging task due to the system's complex higher-order terms. The paper presents a new approach to overcome this difficulty, which is based on the combination of the Backlund transformation and the B\"acklund equation. The solutions of the higher-order Broer-Kaup system are also applied to the study of the related system of the Dym equation, which is a reduction of the higher-order Broer-Kaup system

The existence of the Euler equations' weak solution is crucial for resolving various fundamental issues, such as the well-posedness problem. A long-standing challenge has been to establish the conservativeness of weak solutions. To address the lack of a straightforward path to energy conservation in the Euler equations, this study presents a direct proof of energy preservation. This is achieved by first establishing that the circulation of any weak solution remains constant. Leveraging the conservation of circulation, we then demonstrate that the energy of the Euler equations remains unchanged. To validate the novelty of the circulation conservation proof, we compare it with existing methods in the literature. Our circulation-preserving proof is distinct from the commonly employed Kelvin-Moore type proof that relies on integration by parts, as we avoid it by defining a semi-flow that preserves circulation under certain integrability assumptions.

The Virtual Reality Cosmos Initiative (VIRUP) is an international collaborative effort encompassing higher education, research, and industry, with a mission to develop cutting-edge space and cosmic discoveries through innovative virtual and augmented reality technologies.

The Data Bricks Cosmic Expedition is an interactive learning tool that teaches
middle school students (8-12 years old) essential data and computer science concepts
through a hands-on, physical experience. By utilizing a customized simulation
software, this tool transforms data into tangible, manipulable objects that allow
kids to explore and understand computer vision concepts, such as object
recognition, in a fun and interactive manner. The platform is equipped with a
user-friendly instructor application, providing educators with valuable tools to
effectively integrate it into their classroom curriculum.

A key aspect of Software Defined Networking (SDN) lies in its ability to separate control and data-plane functions, allowing for greater flexibility in managing network traffic. However, this separation introduces new challenges related to data-paths, which are essential for efficient packet forwarding. In SDN environments, these data-paths are created using data-plane programming and flow entries, but they are often complex, dynamic, and difficult to analyze due to the underlying programming models and forwarding engine specifics. Our research focuses on developing a novel approach to identify relevant data-paths in SDN systems by analyzing flow entries, and we have identified key characteristics of data-paths in different SDN architectures. Through experiments on an OpenFlow switch simulator, we have demonstrated the feasibility of our approach and confirmed its effectiveness in reducing the number of irrelevant data-paths.

Strongly relational intelligence enables systems to grasp complex, high-level concepts by recognizing patterns of relevance between different data elements. In this study, we investigate the connection between relational intelligence and disentanglement learning, a technique used to extract independent, semi-independent latent factors from data. Our research reveals that a disentangled representation can be viewed as a specialized form of relational knowledge graph, where each connection represents a distinct relationship between a particular factor. A straightforward method for generating disentanglement by leveraging relational relationships is proposed, and it is demonstrated that a representation can be disentangled from end-to-end if relational relationships can be effectively learned. A novel relational learning algorithm is developed to enhance the disentanglement process, and experiments on multiple datasets confirm that this approach produces more accurate disentanglement and, conversely, that disentanglement enhances the ability to learn relational relationships.

A novel oscillating foil concept in ocean energy harvesting involves moving a series of foils through the water using a central oscillating hub, which creates a complex wake that can transfer energy from the hub to the trailing foils. Research has shown that the secondary foils can capture this energy by oscillating in a synchronized manner. This study focuses on understanding how the secondary foils' performance is affected by their position in the wake and proposes a new approach to maximize their efficiency by adjusting their phase and amplitude in relation to the hub, rather than replicating its natural motion. By adjusting their phase difference, the secondary foils can increase their energy collection efficiency and withstand the harsh conditions of the wake. This method is particularly useful for its adaptability, as it allows the secondary foils to operate in a more stable environment than that created by the hub. Numerical simulations have been conducted to validate these findings and confirm the potential of this technique in improving the efficiency of multiple oscillating foils in a series arrangement.

We've developed a Bayesian method to estimate real-time dynamics for QCD thermodynamics. This approach uses lattice simulations to sample real-time observables and inform our estimates with the result. This method is particularly useful for estimating non-instantaneous correlation functions, which are crucial for understanding phenomena such as meson formation in a thermal environment. This formation is a critical process in our research. Unlike traditional methods, our Bayesian method allows us to accurately set the uncertainty for our estimates and provide a clear uncertainty range. This is achieved by calculating the posterior probability distribution of the model parameters. We have developed a novel method, using a Markov Chain, to accurately determine the uncertainty for our estimates. We have tested our Bayesian method using the spectral function of the vector current, and found that it yields precise and meaningful uncertainty estimates. This method is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of real-time problems in QCD thermodynamics.

The phenomenon of charge-tunneling between a quantum dot and a superconducting material is examined in this study. The interplay between resonant and off-resonant charge transfer is investigated through the variation of the quantum dot's charge at fixed energy levels. By adjusting the voltage of control electrodes, researchers can manipulate the energy of the quantum dot's states and the associated Coulomb blockade. Utilizing a superconducting terminal as a sensing device, researchers have successfully monitored the changes in the quantum dot's energy levels as the terminal's order parameter responds to the modified energy. The resulting data reveal the distinct effects of resonant and off-resonant charge transfer on the quantum dot's dynamics, which are further supported by theoretical models.

In the field of generative models, specifically within the realm of generative models for molecular chemistry, the primary objective is to develop a probabilistic model that effectively generates diverse, viable molecular structures. To achieve this, the research draws upon the concept of energy-based models, utilizing quantum chemistry energy as a key indicator of molecular quality. The study presents a novel approach, known as the adversarial energy autoencoder (AE2), a generative model based on the combination of two adversarial energy models. The first energy function is trained to produce energy values consistent with target compounds, while the second energy function is tasked with distinguishing between target and non-target molecules. The study demonstrates AE2's capacity to produce high-quality, diverse molecular structures through the use of a two-layer auto-encoder framework. The results show that AE2 outperforms multiple baseline models in multiple molecular chemistry tasks, while also showcasing the ability to identify and refine promising lead compounds using AE2-generated molecular data.

We present DTI-M, a high-performance abstract machine for evaluating purely functional programs written in a style that leverages structural editing to represent program transformations. DTI-M builds upon the TOIL framework, incorporating dynamic program structure and token-directed evaluation to facilitate efficient compilation and runtime execution. DTI-M's internal data structure allows for rapid identification of program locations, enabling optimizations such as cache utilisation and reduced pattern matching overhead. DTI-M-Multilisp is a functional programming language, incorporating modules, conditional compilation, and separate compilation, which can be implemented using DTI-M, yielding efficient and compact code in native machine code.

We have analyzed the movement of the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC), accounting for the satellite's spatial structure and external influences. Our research, based on the data from the Vienna Survey of the Magellanic Clouds, utilized a new method to accurately represent the satellite's spatial structure and account for the impact of the Small Magellanic Cloud. The results show that the LMC is moving away from us, with a significant portion of the satellite's outer regions moving faster than the rest. This is different from the satellite's central regions, which are influenced by the satellite's bar and rotation. Our research also found that the satellite's movement towards the Small Magellanic Cloud is consistent with the satellite's interaction with the satellite. However, the satellite's movement towards the Small Magellanic Cloud is not sufficient to explain the satellite's current shape and structure. Our research indicates that the satellite's interaction with the interstellar medium in the satellite is the primary cause of the satellite's current shape and structure.

Significant progress has been made in detecting energy theft using smart meter data and neural networks. However, the effectiveness of these models is often hindered by the lack of sufficient training data and the need for manual optimization of neural network parameters. This research addresses these limitations by developing a novel, automated approach to energy theft detection that utilizes smart meter data and employs recurrent neural networks and a Monte-Carlo based method to automate the selection of the best-performing model. The proposed system is trained on a large dataset of 1000 smart meters and is tested using an independent dataset of 2000 smart meters. The experimental results show that the proposed system significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving a higher accuracy rate of 0.98% in energy theft detection.

We generate a series of surface-specific graphs with embedding density $\Omega(1/n\cdot \sqrt{n})$, achieving the highest known non-constant density at that scale. Our method involves the use of inductive techniques, incorporating cross-pairs and Steiner vertices. Furthermore, we present a surface-independent inductive method for constructing graphs with embedding density $\Omega(1/n\cdot \sqrt{n})$, which can be applied to any graph class with bounded local degrees.

The lifetimes of the $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ and $\Xi^{0}_{c}$ baryons, generated quickly
in combination with hadrons, have been measured at the LHCb detector in collisions
between protons and protons at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. These measurements
are based on data, recorded using baryons that have been paired with D0 mesons produced
within a specific range of transverse momentum and within a particular decay region
stretching up to 30 degrees from the central direction. Following the initial assessment,
which was based on a limited data set, the properties of these baryons were re-measured
using the entire available data collection from 2015 and 2016. These findings have now
been combined with earlier measurements of the $\Xi^{0}_{c}$ lifetime, allowing a more
precise determination of both lifetimes. The results show that the $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ lives
for 96.4 picoseconds or less, the $\Xi^{0}_{c}$ lives for 117.6 picoseconds or less,
both measured at a 68% confidence level. These findings are considered to be the most
precise and accurate to date.

Hyperspectral image classification is a critical process used in remote sensing, yet it faces significant challenges when dealing with large datasets. This is because these large datasets often contain redundant information, making standard classification methods inefficient. Subspace clustering techniques have been successful in reducing dimensionality in remote sensing, yet current approaches fail to effectively handle noise and large datasets due to their reliance on manual parameter tuning and limited ability to incorporate noise tolerance. This paper presents a new framework for similarity-boosted subspace clustering that leverages a novel adaptive spectral subspace clustering method, optimized for the sparse subspace clustering algorithm. This framework utilizes a novel similarity metric to enhance the effectiveness of subspace learning and data representation.
